ideas.script:
### Open

My supervisor recommended Elicit to me, which is an AI tool for finding and reading research papers.

But right now, the tool I'm using for my master's thesis is Claude Science.

It's a new research app from Anthropic, the company that makes Claude.

So in this video, I'll show you what Claude Science is, what it can do for a thesis, one setting you should turn on, where it can go wrong, and how it compares with Elicit.

This isn't sponsored. I just use it.

### What Claude Science is

So what is Claude Science?

Claude Science is a desktop app from Anthropic for doing research, and Anthropic calls it an AI workbench for scientists.

It came out on the 30th of June 2026, and as of October 2026 it's still in beta, which means it's still being tested and changed.

You install it on your own computer, separately from the normal Claude app, and it works on Mac, Windows and Linux.

Then you describe a research task in plain language, and Claude writes code and runs it on your computer to do the work.

For example, you could say, "Here's a folder with my survey results. Clean them up and show me how the answers differ across the three groups."

*[on screen: "Here's a folder with my survey results. Clean them up and show me how the answers differ across the three groups."]*

Claude writes the Python or R code for that, runs it in a sandbox, and gives you back the table and the chart.

A sandbox is a closed-off space where the code can run without touching anything you haven't allowed.

And Claude has to ask you before it opens a new folder or connects to a new website.

Everything it makes, like a figure, a table or a notebook, gets saved with its history.

So you can see the code that made it, and the conversation that led to it.

Think of it like a lab notebook that writes itself while you work.

If your supervisor asks you where a number came from, the answer is right there.

It also connects to scientific databases.

Most of those are for the life sciences, like genes, proteins and chemistry.

But some work for any field, like the one that searches research papers through OpenAlex and arXiv, and there's a literature review skill that helps Claude find papers, check them and pull them together.

Claude Science comes with the paid Claude plans, which are Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise, and it isn't on the free plan.

As of October 2026, Pro is 20 dollars a month in the US, and the price can be different where you live.

And it has a feature that checks Claude's own work, which I'll show you in a minute, along with a setting you should change if you're on Pro.

### What Claude Science can do for a thesis

So what can Claude Science actually do for a master's thesis?

My thesis is for my master's in Human-Computer Interaction at Tallinn University, and it's on the invisible cognitive cost of switching between productivity tools.

For a thesis like mine, these are the parts I think matter most.

The first one is finding papers.

It can search OpenAlex, which is a big free catalogue of research papers, and arXiv, where a lot of computer science papers go first.

The second one is reading them.

When a paper is open access, which means it's free to read, Claude can get the full text by itself.

For papers behind a paywall, you can add your library's login details in the app, and then it can reach what your university already pays for, and nothing more.

The third one is working with your own data.

If you have survey answers or measurements, it can clean them, run the analysis and make the figures, and keep the code that did it.

And the fourth one is writing.

You can draft in it, and it shows you a preview of Markdown and LaTeX, which a lot of theses are written in.

Anthropic describes Claude Science as an app that "integrates the tools and packages that researchers most commonly use."

And since my thesis is literally about switching between tools, I notice that.

Research can't tell me yet whether one app doing everything makes the switching cheaper for your brain, and that's the kind of question my field asks.

### The Claude Science reviewer, and the setting to turn on

The feature in Claude Science I'd point students to first is the reviewer.

The reviewer is a second check that runs after Claude answers.

It reads back what Claude said, the plan you approved, the files it saved, and the record of the code that actually ran, and then it checks if they all match.

Anthropic's docs give some examples of what it catches.

A result reported as computed when nothing ran.

A citation that doesn't support the claim it's attached to.

And a reference whose DOI leads to a different article.

*[on screen: The reviewer can flag: a result reported when nothing ran / a citation that doesn't support the claim / a DOI that leads to a different article / a plan step that wasn't done]*

A DOI is like a permanent web address for a research paper.

So if the address in the reference opens a different paper, something is wrong with that reference.

This matters a lot for students, because AI tools have made up references before, and they've cited real papers for things those papers never said.

When the reviewer finds something, a small card shows up under the message, and Claude has to either fix the problem or explain why it doesn't apply.

Now the setting.

On the Max, Team and Enterprise plans, the automatic reviewer is on by default.

On the Pro plan, it starts off, and you turn it on for each session.

*[on screen: Auto-review: on by default on Max, Team, Enterprise / OFF by default on Pro, turn it on per session]*

So if you're on Pro, turn it on.

Reviews also use your plan's usage, so they count towards your limits.

### Where Claude Science can go wrong

Claude Science can still get things wrong, and Anthropic says so in its own docs.

Their exact words are, "The reviewer reduces, but doesn't eliminate, errors."

And they tell you to verify results before you rely on them in research or publication.

So I want to go through the limits I'd want a friend to know about.

The first one is that the reviewer checks whether Claude's claims match what ran, and that's all.

It doesn't re-run the analysis, and it doesn't judge whether the method was the right choice for your research question.

For example, say you compare two groups with the wrong statistical test.

The reviewer can confirm the test really ran and the numbers in the answer match the output.

It won't tell you that a different test was the right one.

That part is still your job, and your supervisor's.

The second one is data from real people.

Your files stay on your computer, but the parts Claude reads are sent to the model as part of the conversation.

So if your thesis has interview recordings, survey answers or anything else from participants, check what your ethics approval and consent forms allow before any AI tool reads it.

*[optional line: And the next two are the ones you only find out after you've started.]*

The third one is usage limits.

Claude Science shares the same limits as the rest of your Claude plan, including normal chats.

On Pro and Max, there's a limit that resets every five hours and a weekly one, and when you hit them, a long analysis pauses until the reset, unless you pay for extra usage.

The fourth one is that it's built mostly for the life sciences.

Most of the ready-made database connections are for biology and chemistry, so if you're in HCI or the social sciences like me, you'll use fewer of them.

Anthropic's docs do say it supports the social sciences, computer science and other fields too.

And the last one is that it's in beta, so things can change or break while you're mid-thesis.

### Claude Science vs Elicit

So how does Claude Science compare with Elicit, the tool my supervisor recommended?

Elicit is an AI research assistant built around research papers.

Its help centre says it searches over 138 million academic papers from Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and PubMed.

It can find papers, summarise them, let you chat with them, and write research reports.

It also has data extraction tables.

Say you have twenty papers on interruptions at work.

You add a column for the sample size, one for the method and one for the main finding, and Elicit fills them in for every paper.

*[on screen: a table, 20 papers as rows / columns: sample size, method, main finding]*

And it helps with systematic reviews, which are reviews that follow a strict, written-down method for finding and screening every relevant study, so someone else could repeat it.

As of October 2026, Elicit Basic is free, with unlimited paper summaries and chats with papers, and two research reports a month.

Elicit Plus is 12 dollars a month, and Elicit Pro is 49 dollars a month.

Elicit has limits too, and its help centre lists them.

For papers behind a paywall, it uses the title and abstract unless you have a subscription and its browser extension, and it doesn't include books or dissertations.

So this is how I'd put the difference.

Elicit is built for finding, screening and comparing papers.

Claude Science is built for doing the research work, like running the analysis on your data, making figures and writing, and reading papers is one part of that.

*[on screen: Elicit: finding, screening and comparing papers. Free plan. / Claude Science: analysis, figures, writing, with papers as one part. Paid Claude plan.]*

So if your thesis is mostly a literature review, Elicit is made for exactly that, and its free plan is a good place to start.

If your thesis has data you have to analyse, Claude Science does a lot more of that part.

And nothing stops you from using both.

### Using Claude Science for your thesis without getting in trouble

If you use Claude Science, or any AI tool, for your thesis, these are the things I'd do to stay out of academic integrity trouble.

First, read your university's AI policy before you start.

At my university, Tallinn University, the AI page says that "failure to make proper reference to the use of AI is considered academic fraud."

I went through my university's rules properly in my video on how I use AI as a master's student, so I'll link it.

Second, tell your supervisor which tool you're using and what for.

They might have rules for your department, and they're the one who signs off on your work.

Third, check every citation yourself, even with the reviewer on.

Open the paper, find the part that's supposed to say what Claude says it says, and read it with your own eyes.

The reviewer is a second pair of eyes, and you're still the first.

Fourth, use the history.

Because every figure and table keeps the code and the conversation behind it, you have a record of exactly how you used AI.

So when your university asks you to describe your AI use, you can be specific.

And fifth, write the parts you're graded on yourself.

The same Tallinn University page says the author is "fully responsible for the content and form of the presented work."

So whatever Claude Science helps with, your name is the one on the thesis.

### My Claude Science verdict

So would I recommend Claude Science for thesis research?

My honest answer is that it depends on what kind of thesis you have.

This is who I think it suits.

If your thesis has data you need to analyse, and you can read enough code to check what it did, Claude Science can do a lot of the heavy lifting, and the history it keeps makes your work easier to explain.

If you're already paying for Claude Pro, it doesn't cost anything extra to try it.

And this is who I'd send somewhere else first.

If your thesis is mostly reading and comparing papers, start with Elicit's free plan, or Google Scholar and your library.

If you can't pay for a Claude plan right now, Claude Science isn't on the free one.

And if you can't read any code at all, I'd be careful, because you'd be trusting an analysis you can't check.

Whichever tool you use, the thesis is still yours, so check the citations and own the method.

So tell me in the comments, are you using an AI tool for your thesis or your research, and which one?

ideas.script:
### Open

Singapore's government has built a dating app.

It's called FirstDate, and it gives you one match at a time, picked by a matching algorithm from 1962.

A while ago I made a video about Ghana's Marrify, the platform where you can check if someone is already married.

Both of these apps are about marriage, but they are very different ideas.

I look at things like this as a UX and HCI person. I'm interested in user privacy, and in how technology finds its way into our lives.

So in this video, I'll show you what Singapore actually launched, how the matching works, what data it holds, and how it compares to Marrify.

And at the end, I'll tell you if I would use it myself.

### What Singapore's FirstDate app is

FirstDate is a dating service run by GovTech, which is Singapore's Government Technology Agency.

GovTech emailed public officers about it on the 29th of September 2026, and it's a pilot.

So as of October 2026, only people who work in Singapore's public service can use it.

Ordinary Singaporeans can't sign up, and GovTech says it hasn't decided whether it will go beyond the pilot.

At the start, you had to be between 21 and 35.

On the 20th of October, they raised the limit to 45 for the second round of sign-ups.

And you have to be single, widowed or divorced.

The idea came out of GovTech's yearly hackathon, which is an event where staff build and test new ideas quickly.

This is how it works.

You sign in with Singpass.

Singpass is Singapore's national digital ID, the login people use for government services.

So every account on FirstDate belongs to a real, verified person.

Then you answer a questionnaire, about 30 questions on your interests, your habits, your values, and what you're looking for.

You can use a nickname instead of your real name.

Then the algorithm gives you one match.

There's no feed of faces to swipe through. You get one person.

You see their profile name, their interests, a compatibility score, and a short note about the match.

You don't see their face.

Both of you get an SMS, and you each have three days to say yes or no.

If you both say yes, FirstDate shares your Telegram contacts with each other.

If either of you says no, that match ends, and you might get another one in a later round.

They also won't match you with someone from your own agency, so you won't be paired with the person who sits next to you at work.

There are optional "date quests," which are suggested things to do on the date, and during some periods there are vouchers for doing them.

And after each match, they send you a survey asking how it went, including whether you actually met in person.

FirstDate's own website says, "Swipe fatigue ends here."

### Why Singapore's government is playing matchmaker

So why would Singapore's government build a dating app?

Most news reports connected it to Singapore's birth rate, and the numbers explain why.

In 2025, Singapore's resident total fertility rate fell to 0.87.

That's the average number of babies a woman is expected to have in her lifetime, and the year before, it was 0.97.

*[on screen: Singapore resident total fertility rate / 2024: 0.97 / 2025: 0.87 / Source: Singapore Department of Statistics]*

For a population to replace itself without immigration, that number usually needs to be around 2.1.

Marriages are falling too.

24,688 marriages were registered in Singapore in 2025, which is 6.2% fewer than in 2024.

And in February, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong warned that if nothing changes, the citizen population could start to shrink by the early 2040s.

To be fair to GovTech, FirstDate's website doesn't mention birth rates at all.

It talks about supporting singles on their dating journey.

But this is also something Singapore's government has done before.

In 1984, it set up the Social Development Unit, because fewer female university graduates were getting married, and the unit helped graduates meet each other.

A year later, another body was set up to do the same for people without degrees, and the two merged in 2009.

So the government matching people is more than 40 years old in Singapore.

FirstDate is the version with Singpass and an algorithm.

And Singapore isn't alone. Tokyo's city government launched its own dating app in 2024, and Seoul runs matchmaking events for young people too.

### How the Gale-Shapley algorithm works

FirstDate matches people with something called the Gale-Shapley algorithm.

It's also called the stable marriage algorithm.

Two mathematicians, David Gale and Lloyd Shapley, published it in 1962.

In 2012, Shapley shared the Nobel Prize in economics with Alvin Roth, for work that includes this kind of matching.

And it's used for serious things.

In the US, versions of it are used to match new doctors to hospitals, and some cities use it to assign children to schools.

So how does it work?

Picture two groups of three people, and everyone ranks the people in the other group, from first choice to last.

*[on screen: preference table]*

*[on screen: code]*

```
Ada:    Tunde, Femi, Kola        Tunde: Bisi, Ada, Chioma
Bisi:   Tunde, Kola, Femi        Femi:  Ada, Chioma, Bisi
Chioma: Femi, Tunde, Kola        Kola:  Ada, Bisi, Chioma
```

In the first round, everyone on one side sends an offer to their first choice.

If you receive offers, you don't say yes yet.

You hold on to the best offer you've got so far, like a "maybe," and you reject the rest.

Then everyone who got rejected sends an offer to their next choice.

And if someone holding a "maybe" gets a better offer, they can drop the old one and keep the new one.

It goes round and round like that until nobody gets rejected anymore, and then everyone is matched.

So in my example, Ada and Bisi both send their first offer to Tunde.

Tunde prefers Bisi, so he holds Bisi and rejects Ada.

Ada tries her second choice, Femi.

Femi was holding Chioma's offer, but he prefers Ada, so he swaps.

Chioma tries Tunde next, but Tunde still prefers Bisi, so Chioma tries Kola, and Kola holds her.

Nobody is rejected anymore, so it stops.

Bisi with Tunde, Ada with Femi, and Chioma with Kola.

*[on screen: code]*

```
// Gale-Shapley stable matching, simplified
function stableMatch(proposers, receivers) {
  const free = Object.keys(proposers); // everyone starts unmatched
  const next = {};                     // where each person is on their list
  const holding = {};                  // receiver -> offer they're holding
  while (free.length) {
    const p = free.shift();
    next[p] = (next[p] ?? -1) + 1;
    const r = proposers[p][next[p]];   // their next choice
    const current = holding[r];
    if (!current) {
      holding[r] = p;                  // first offer: "maybe"
    } else if (receivers[r].indexOf(p) < receivers[r].indexOf(current)) {
      holding[r] = p;                  // better offer: swap
      free.push(current);
    } else {
      free.push(p);                    // worse offer: rejected
    }
  }
  return holding;
}
// returns { Tunde: "Bisi", Femi: "Ada", Kola: "Chioma" }
```

The important word here is "stable."

A matching is stable when there are no two people who would both rather be with each other than with the person they got.

Chioma would have preferred Femi or Tunde, but both of them prefer the person they already have.

So nobody has a reason to break away from their match.

There's one more detail that matters.

Gale and Shapley showed that the side sending the offers gets the best partner it could get in any stable matching.

So who sends the offers matters.

GovTech hasn't said how FirstDate turns your questionnaire answers into a ranking, or which side sends the offers, so I can't tell you that part.

And a stable match on paper is still only on paper.

FirstDate's own website says compatibility on paper doesn't guarantee chemistry.

### What data FirstDate collects and who sees it

When I made my Marrify video, the question I kept asking was who can see your data, and how much of it.

So I looked at Singapore's FirstDate the same way.

This is what GovTech holds about you if you sign up.

It knows who you really are, because you logged in with Singpass.

It knows you're single and looking.

It has your answers about your interests, your habits, your values and your preferences.

It knows who you were matched with, and from the survey, whether you went on the date.

And this is who sees what.

Your profile is only visible to your current match.

Your contact details are only shared if both of you say yes.

And your match doesn't see your face before deciding.

FirstDate says your data is handled under government data security standards, and that it won't be sold or shared with third parties, unless the law requires or allows it.

You can also deactivate your account and ask for your information to be removed.

In my Marrify video, I talked about data minimisation, which means showing only the minimum data needed to answer the question.

FirstDate is close to that.

Your match only sees what they need to decide on one date.

*[optional line: And this next part is the one I didn't expect when I started reading about it.]*

There's one thing to know about the law, though.

Singapore's main data protection law, the PDPA, doesn't apply to government agencies.

Public agencies follow other rules instead, including the Public Sector (Governance) Act.

Singapore's government told Parliament in 2019 that these rules set standards comparable to the PDPA, if not higher.

And at that time, a public officer who misused data could face a fine of up to 5,000 dollars, or up to two years in jail, or both.

So for me, the bigger question is who's holding the data.

Everyone using FirstDate works for the government.

So your dating answers sit with the government, and the government is also your employer.

### Singapore's FirstDate vs Ghana's Marrify

So how does Singapore's FirstDate compare with Ghana's Marrify?

A quick reminder of Marrify, in case you haven't seen that video.

It launched in Accra at the end of August 2026.

It's run by a private company, Marry Right Ghana Limited, in partnership with Ghana's Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection.

It pulls marriage and divorce records from the Registrar-General's Department, the courts, local assemblies and the Ghana Gazette.

So you can check whether someone already has a marriage on record, and whether a pastor, an imam or a venue is licensed to conduct a marriage.

The founder, Dennis Adjei Dwomoh, said at the launch that you can find that information for free.

Since my video, I've also seen reports that it has an AI assistant that answers questions about Ghanaian marriage law.

And as of October 2026, the database is still being filled, so an empty search doesn't prove that someone has never married.

Now, the differences.

The first difference is the purpose.

FirstDate helps you meet someone, and Marrify helps you check someone.

The second difference is who's behind it.

FirstDate is built by a government agency.

Marrify is a private company working with a ministry, using records that come from government offices and the courts.

The third difference is whose data it is, and to me this is the biggest one.

On FirstDate, every piece of data comes from someone who chose to sign up.

On Marrify, the records are about people who never signed up for anything.

Their marriage or divorce was registered somewhere, and now it can be searched.

The fourth difference is who can see it.

On FirstDate, only your match sees your profile.

Marrify is built for the public to search.

And the fifth difference is how each one builds trust.

FirstDate checks who you are with Singpass.

Marrify pulls from official records, so you don't have to rely on what someone tells you about themselves.

*[on screen: comparison table]*

*[on screen: code]*

```
                FirstDate (Singapore)          Marrify (Ghana)
Purpose         meet someone                   check someone
Run by          GovTech (government agency)    Marry Right Ghana Ltd + Ministry of Gender
Whose data      people who signed up           people in official records
Who sees it     only your current match        built for the public to search
Trust comes     Singpass ID check              official records
from
```

### What these two apps say about Singapore and Ghana

I always say that technology is not neutral.

It works in the system you use it in.

And I think Singapore's FirstDate and Ghana's Marrify show you a lot about the countries they were built in.

In Singapore, I think the problem FirstDate is trying to solve is that fewer people are meeting and marrying, and the government is worried about what that means for the future.

And the solution expects people to trust their government enough to log in with their national ID and tell it what they want in a partner.

Tingting Liu, a researcher at the University of Technology Sydney, described it as "a particularly Singaporean faith in systems."

In Ghana, I think the problem Marrify is trying to solve is different.

The records already exist, but they're spread across different offices, and it's possible for someone to hide a marriage.

Ghana's minister, Dr Agnes Naa Momo Lartey, said the effectiveness of a platform like this "will ultimately depend on public confidence in the information it provides."

So in Singapore, the trust question is about you trusting the government with your data.

In Ghana, it's about trusting the information you find about someone else.

### The case against a government dating app

Now, the strongest case against a government dating app like FirstDate.

The first point is about the state in your private life.

According to the BBC, some Singaporeans called the pilot "dystopian."

Pan Wang, an associate professor at the University of New South Wales, said the government is "taking the role of big parent."

The second point is whether it will change anything.

Pan Wang also said it "may not necessarily help to address the decline in birthrates," because causes like housing costs, living costs and work pressure are still there.

And Teo Kai Xiang, a former Straits Times journalist, told Al Jazeera that cost is a bigger barrier to dating than a lack of matchmaking.

The third point is the matching itself.

Jean Liu, a psychology professor at the Singapore Institute of Technology, said questionnaires are limited in how well they predict who you'll click with, and that the process may break down if too few people sign up.

She also said the most useful part might be the government studying and publishing what it learns about dating, which dating app companies rarely do.

The fourth point is that it leaves most people out, because only public officers can use it.

And on the Marrify side, the fair point is that the harm it prevents is serious.

Finding out after your wedding that your partner was already married is a real thing that happens to people.

And Marrify's records come from official sources, where they were already public in some form.

So this is where I land.

Personally, I wouldn't use FirstDate.

I don't want an algorithm to find my love.

I've tried dating apps, and I didn't like them. And I don't think the love of my life is on a dating app.

But I'm still very interested in it, because I look at this as a UX and HCI person, and I care about user privacy and how technology finds its way into our lives.

So tell me, if your government built a dating app, would you sign up?

ideas.script:
### Open

I have never signed up on Truecaller.

But I've seen Truecaller show my name.

And if you've never downloaded it either, your name can still show up on someone's screen when you call them.

Truecaller is such a very interesting product, because you don't have to sign up on Truecaller for it to know who you are.

In this video, I'll show you where that name comes from, what a Lagos court said about it in September 2026, and how to take your number off Truecaller.

### How Truecaller gets your name

So how does Truecaller get your name, even if you never signed up?

Before I made this video, the way I believed Truecaller worked is that it gets contacts from people that sign up.

So you sign up, and Truecaller gets your whole phone book.

I went and checked, and that's partly right.

Truecaller has a few sources for the names it shows, so I'll name them all quickly and then explain the three big ones.

*[on screen: where Truecaller's names come from / shared contacts (Enhanced Search) / names people suggest / users' own profiles / spam reports / public business listings]*

There are people who share their contacts with Truecaller.

There are names that people suggest for a number after a call.

There are users' own profiles, because when you sign up, you put in your own name.

There are spam reports from the community.

And there are public business listings.

The first big one is shared contacts.

For years, uploaded phone books were one of the main ways Truecaller built its database.

Today, Truecaller calls this feature Enhanced Search.

If a user turns it on, the numbers in their phone book, and the names they saved them with, go to Truecaller's servers.

So if your friend saved you as "Gbemi Tallinn" and shared their contacts, Truecaller now has your number next to "Gbemi Tallinn".

*[on screen: code]*

```
{
  "shared_by": "+2348031112222",
  "contacts": [
    { "number": "+2348059876543", "saved_as": "Gbemi Tallinn" },
    { "number": "+2348067778888", "saved_as": "Tunde Mechanic" }
  ]
}
```

*[on screen: a simplified illustration of shared contacts, not Truecaller's real format]*

Now this is where I was wrong, or at least not fully right.

Truecaller has said since at least 2018 that the versions you download from the Google Play Store and the Apple App Store don't upload your phone book.

And in the Lagos court case I'll talk about in a minute, Truecaller told the court that contacts only get uploaded if a user takes a separate, voluntary step.

In 2024, Hong Kong's Consumer Council tested this, and they found the same thing.

Truecaller uploaded contact lists only after they installed the version from Truecaller's own website and turned on Enhanced Search.

But there's another side to it.

In 2022, Rest of World reported that on some phones where Truecaller came already installed, Enhanced Search was ticked by default.

And everything people shared over the years is still part of how the database got this big.

The second big source is name suggestions.

After a call from a number Truecaller doesn't know well, the app can ask you to suggest a name for it.

So a stranger you called once can type a name for your number, and that name can become part of what Truecaller knows about you.

The third big source is spam reports.

When enough people mark a number as spam, Truecaller labels it for everyone.

That's the part most of us like, because it's how you know that unknown number is a loan app calling you for the fifth time.

### How a Truecaller lookup works

So what happens when a Truecaller user gets a call from your number?

The app takes your number and looks it up.

It checks the phone's own contacts first, and if your number isn't there, it asks Truecaller's servers who this number belongs to.

The servers might have your number saved under many different names, from many different people.

So Truecaller has to pick one.

Truecaller hasn't published exactly how it picks, so I can't show you their real logic.

But to show you the idea, if I were building something like this, the simplest version would be to pick the name most people saved you as.

*[on screen: code]*

```
SELECT saved_as, COUNT(*) AS times_saved
FROM shared_contacts
WHERE number = '+2348059876543'
GROUP BY saved_as
ORDER BY times_saved DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

*[on screen: a simplified illustration of the idea, not Truecaller's real code]*

If thirty people saved you as "Gbemi" and two people saved you as "Gbemi Landlord", this query gives you "Gbemi".

In 2022, Truecaller told Rest of World that people sharing their contacts makes its algorithm more accurate, and this is the kind of thing they mean.

More people saving your number means more names to choose from.

It also explains why Truecaller sometimes shows a name that's wrong, or a name that's a bit embarrassing.

If the only person who saved your number saved you as "Mummy's Tailor", that might be what strangers see.

One more thing Truecaller said in court is that the app only lets you search a number to get a name.

So you need someone's number first, and then it tells you the name.

You can't type a name and get someone's number back, at least in the app versions Truecaller described to the court.

### Why Truecaller is a privacy question

The privacy question with Truecaller is about people who never signed up.

If I share my contacts with Truecaller, I've agreed to Truecaller's terms.

But the two hundred people in my phone book didn't agree to anything.

Their numbers, and the names I saved them as, go to a company they may never have heard of.

Privacy groups have been saying this for years.

When Privacy International asked Truecaller about it in 2019, Truecaller pointed non-users to its unlisting option.

And Privacy International's answer, as TechCabal reported it, was that unlisting only helps people who already know they're in the database.

In September 2019, Nigeria's NITDA, the National Information Technology Development Agency, said it had started an investigation into Truecaller.

NITDA said Truecaller's privacy policy wasn't in line with Nigeria's data protection rules at the time, and that it "collects far more information than it needs to provide its primary service."

NITDA also said more than seven million Nigerians were using Truecaller back then.

And it pointed out something I found really interesting.

Nigerian users were covered by Truecaller's Indian company, with a different privacy policy from the one for users in Europe.

Europe is where this gets different.

Because of GDPR, the EU's data protection law, Truecaller said in 2022 that Enhanced Search is only offered to users outside the EU, and that contact data from the EU gets rejected.

And in September 2025, Truecaller, which is a Swedish company, announced that Sweden's data protection authority had closed an investigation into it, saying the investigation didn't show a GDPR breach.

So the same app can treat your contacts differently depending on where you are.

### The Truecaller court case in Lagos

Truecaller has been to court in Nigeria more than once, and the most recent case was decided in Lagos on the 14th of September, 2026.

*[optional line: And stay for how this case ended, because both sides walked away with something.]*

The case was at the Lagos State High Court, before Justice N. O. Ojuromi.

It was brought by the Data Privacy Lawyers Association, for its members who don't use Truecaller, together with two named applicants.

Their lawyer was Olumide Babalola.

One of the applicants, Esther Odunze, said that around March 2025, a vendor she'd never dealt with told her he'd found her name and number on Truecaller.

And she said she had never registered on Truecaller or given them her number.

They sued Truecaller International LLP, which is Truecaller's company in India.

They asked the court to stop Truecaller from processing the numbers of non-users without consent, to delete that data, and to pay three hundred million naira in damages.

*[on screen: Lagos State High Court / judgment 14 September 2026 / Data Privacy Lawyers Association v Truecaller International LLP / ₦200m general + ₦100m exemplary damages asked for]*

Truecaller argued that the Lagos court had no jurisdiction, because it operates from India and has no office or servers in Nigeria.

It argued that users give consent, and that contacts only get uploaded when a user chooses to share them.

And it pointed out that one applicant's number was already public on Instagram, and another looked like a business number.

So what did the court decide?

First, the judge said the court did have jurisdiction, because data protection is part of your right to privacy under Section 37 of the Nigerian Constitution.

Second, and this is the part I think matters most, the court said a user's consent does not cover the people in their contacts.

In the judge's words, as The ICIR reported from the court's certified copy, "Consent to one does not equate to consent to the other."

So your friend agreeing to Truecaller's terms is not you agreeing.

But then the court dismissed the case.

The judge said the applicants didn't prove, with evidence, that they had suffered harm.

The judgment says "the mere misappropriation of personal information, without a resultant economic harm," isn't enough on its own.

So nobody got damages, and the court didn't order Truecaller to delete non-users' data.

The court did note that Truecaller had already deleted the applicants' own numbers after they asked.

And after the judgment, their lawyer said the applicants plan to appeal the part about harm.

That's how things stand as of October 2026.

*[on screen: what the Lagos court said / a user's consent is not their contacts' consent / but no proven harm, so the case was dismissed / applicants say they'll appeal]*

If you're wondering whether this was the first Nigerian case, it wasn't.

In 2017, a Nigerian named Daniel John sued Truecaller in Lagos, also with Olumide Babalola's firm, and the High Court struck it out in 2018 over jurisdiction and how the papers were served. It went to the Court of Appeal, and I couldn't find how that ended.

Then in 2024, BusinessDay reported a Federal High Court ruling in Abuja that went Truecaller's way.

That court said the users who shared their contacts were the ones responsible for that data, and not Truecaller.

The Lagos judge went the other way and treated Truecaller as responsible.

And in March 2025, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, the NDPC, said it was investigating Truecaller. I couldn't find a public result of that yet.

So in Nigeria, this isn't settled, and an appeal court will probably have the final say.

### Truecaller's side of the story

To be fair to Truecaller, there's a real reason millions of Nigerians use it.

Truecaller's own data says that in 2025, 51% of unknown calls Nigerians got were spam or fraud, the highest share in Africa in their report.

When you get calls like that every day, an app that tells you who's calling is useful.

After the Lagos judgment, Truecaller put out a statement, which TechCabal reported.

They said, "We welcome the court's recognition that caller identification and spam detection serve an important public-safety purpose."

They also said, "Anyone, whether or not they use Truecaller, can remove their number from our service at any time."

Truecaller also says consent isn't its only legal basis.

Under Section 25 of the Nigeria Data Protection Act, a company can also process data for legitimate interests or the public interest, and Truecaller says caller ID and spam protection fall there.

The Lagos court said legitimate interest has limits when it clashes with someone's rights.

And Truecaller said it won't suspend or redesign its service in Nigeria.

I have never signed up on Truecaller, and I've still seen it show my name.

I look at this as a UX and HCI person. I'm interested in user privacy, and in how technology finds its way into our lives.

It's the same reason I made my videos on Ghana's Marrify and on how Uber serves millions of translations from memory.

So this is what I think.

I think the spam protection is useful, and I understand why people install it.

I think the weak spot is the people who never signed up, because they're the ones whose names are in there without anyone asking them.

And I think the court saying a user's consent isn't their contacts' consent is the most important line in that whole judgment, even though Truecaller won the case.

### What developers can learn from Truecaller

If you're a developer building an app that asks for contacts, the Truecaller case has a lesson for you too.

When your user taps "Allow" on contacts, that's your user's consent.

According to the Lagos court, it isn't the consent of everyone in their phone book.

So before you upload anyone's contacts, ask if you really need them on your server at all.

A lot of contact features can run on the phone itself, without sending the whole phone book anywhere.

The second lesson is about hashing phone numbers.

After the ruling, Truecaller said that when someone unlists, it keeps a one-way hash of that number, so the number doesn't get added back the next time a user shares their contacts.

A hash turns a value into a fixed string that you can't turn back into the original directly.

That's a good idea, and I want to add one thing every developer should know.

Phone numbers are easy to guess, because there aren't that many of them.

Moxie Marlinspike, who founded Signal, wrote in 2014 that "There are only roughly 10^10 phone numbers," which is about ten billion.

*[on screen: "There are only roughly 10^10 phone numbers" / "Inverting these hashes is basically a straightforward dictionary attack." / Moxie Marlinspike, Signal blog, 2014]*

And he wrote that "inverting these hashes is basically a straightforward dictionary attack."

That means if someone gets a list of plain hashed phone numbers, they can hash every possible number and match them up.

Truecaller says its hash can't be reversed, and I don't know how they built it, so I'm not saying theirs is weak.

I'm saying that if you build something like this yourself, a plain hash isn't enough.

If you're using Laravel, for example, you can use a keyed hash, with a secret key that only your server knows.

*[on screen: code]*

```
// a plain hash of a phone number (easy to guess back)
$plain = hash('sha256', '+2348059876543');

// a keyed hash, with a secret only your server knows
$keyed = hash_hmac('sha256', '+2348059876543', config('services.phone_hash_key'));

// keep unlisted numbers out when someone shares contacts
$isUnlisted = UnlistedNumber::where('number_hash', $keyed)->exists();
```

Without the secret key, someone with your list can't just hash every number and compare.

### How to remove your number from Truecaller

If you want to take your number off Truecaller, you can do it even if you've never used the app.

Truecaller's unlisting page is at truecaller.com/unlisting.

*[on screen: truecaller.com/unlisting / enter your number with +234 / complete the check / tap Unlist, then confirm]*

You enter your phone number with your country code, so +234 for Nigeria.

You complete the little check that you're not a robot, tap Unlist, and confirm it.

Guides I found say it can take up to 24 hours.

If you do have a Truecaller account, you have to deactivate it in the app first, under Settings and then Privacy Center, and then unlist on the website.

And once you're unlisted, you can't use Truecaller to search numbers with that number, because you've taken yourself out.

Truecaller says it keeps that hash of your number, so you don't get added back when someone shares their contacts again.

Unlisting doesn't change what your friends saved you as in their own phones.

And it doesn't touch other caller ID apps, or any other website that has your number.

I think unlisting should be easier to find, because most people who need it don't even know they're on Truecaller.

So now you know where to look.

Tell me in the comments, would you unlist your number, or do you think the spam protection is worth it?

ideas.title: Why the US Is Banning Chinese AI (and the Hypocrisy in It)
ideas.format: Talking head + receipts (#07, #21): the DHS order, the Navy email and the Texas ban as receipt cards in date order on a simple timeline. Shorts: white rounded box, black heavy lowercase title (T3).

ideas.hook: In October 2026, the US government ordered every civilian federal agency to remove DeepSeek, the Chinese AI chatbot, from its systems.
ideas.summary: A news-and-opinion kit on the US bans on DeepSeek, built on the October 2026 DHS order that told every civilian federal agency to remove it. Every fact is dated and sourced as of 26 October 2026.

record.where: Desk, a plain wall behind you.
record.how: Sitting, chest up, measured news voice; your opinion part slower. Read from the teleprompter, phone sideways (16:9) on a stand at eye level.
record.props: Laptop with the DHS order open.

ideas.script:
### Open

In October 2026, the US government ordered every civilian federal agency to remove DeepSeek, the Chinese AI chatbot, from its systems.

The reason they give is that your data could end up with the Chinese government.

AI is so technical. But it's also such a political thing.

I find this whole thing very interesting, and I feel like there's a lot of hypocrisy in it.

For the record, all my devices are Apple, and I haven't used DeepSeek myself.

So I'll show you what was banned and why, the best argument for it, where I think the hypocrisy is, and what it means for us in Nigeria.

### What the US actually banned

So what exactly has the US banned when it comes to Chinese AI?

Mostly one company, DeepSeek.

DeepSeek is an AI company from Hangzhou in China, and in January 2025, its chatbot app went to number one on Apple's App Store in the US.

On the 24th of January 2025, the US Navy sent an email telling its people not to use DeepSeek "in any capacity."

The House of Representatives told congressional offices that DeepSeek was "under review" and "currently unauthorized for official House use."

NASA barred it from agency devices and networks, and the Pentagon's IT agency blocked the website.

Then the states joined in.

Texas banned DeepSeek on state devices on the 31st of January 2025, along with RedNote and Lemon8.

New York followed on the 10th of February, and Virginia on the 11th.

In Congress, two lawmakers, Josh Gottheimer and Darin LaHood, introduced a bill called the No DeepSeek on Government Devices Act. As of October 2026, it still hasn't made it out of committee.

And then came the biggest one.

On the 19th of October 2026, the Department of Homeland Security made public an order that was signed back in July.

It tells every civilian federal agency to remove DeepSeek products from their systems and stop buying them.

It even covers other companies' products that are built on DeepSeek.

*[on screen: Jan 2025 Navy, House, NASA, Pentagon / Jan to Feb 2025 Texas, New York, Virginia / Feb 2025 No DeepSeek on Government Devices Act (still in committee) / Oct 2026 DHS order for all civilian federal agencies]*

One thing I want to be clear about.

All of these bans are about government devices, government systems and government contracts.

If you're an ordinary person in the US, or in Nigeria, nothing here stops you from downloading DeepSeek and using it.

### Why the US says it banned DeepSeek

So why does the US say it banned DeepSeek?

There are four main reasons, and other countries gave some of the same ones.

The first reason is where your data goes.

DeepSeek's own privacy policy said the information it collects is "stored in secure servers located in the People's Republic of China."

*[on screen: DeepSeek privacy policy: "stored in secure servers located in the People's Republic of China"]*

And the new DHS order says using DeepSeek "may result in the transfer of sensitive data to the PRC if used by U.S. government employees or vendors."

The second reason is a Chinese law.

China's National Intelligence Law, from 2017, says in Article 7 that "All organizations and citizens shall support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts in accordance with law."

The same article says they have to keep that intelligence work secret.

*[on screen: National Intelligence Law, Article 7 (China Law Translate)]*

Think of it like this.

You keep your diary at a friend's house, and your friend's country has a law that says if intelligence officers ask for anything in the house, your friend has to help them and keep quiet about it.

Your friend might be a very nice person. The law still applies to them.

That's the worry with a Chinese company holding your data.

The third reason is security.

In January 2025, a security company called Wiz found one of DeepSeek's databases open on the internet, with chat history inside it.

And in September 2025, a US government AI centre called CAISI tested DeepSeek's models.

With a common jailbreak trick, DeepSeek's R1-0528 model went along with 94% of clearly harmful requests. The American models they compared it to went along with 8%.

The fourth reason is censorship.

When New York banned it, Governor Kathy Hochul talked about protecting people from "state-sponsored censorship."

And that same CAISI report found that DeepSeek's models "echoed four times as many inaccurate and misleading CCP narratives as U.S. reference models did." CCP means the Chinese Communist Party.

*[on screen: CAISI, Sept 2025 / jailbreak: 94% vs 8% / CCP narratives: 4x]*

And it wasn't only the US.

Italy's data protection authority blocked DeepSeek on the 30th of January 2025. DeepSeek had told them European privacy law didn't apply to it, and the authority disagreed.

South Korea paused new downloads for about two months over how the app handled personal data.

And Australia and Taiwan banned it on government devices.

### The strongest case for banning DeepSeek

Before I tell you where I think the hypocrisy is, I want to give the best argument for banning DeepSeek on government devices, because a lot of it is fair.

First, governments lock down their devices for American AI too.

In 2023, the US House of Representatives limited staff to the paid version of ChatGPT, for certain tasks only.

In 2024, it told staff they couldn't use Microsoft's Copilot.

And Italy, the same country that blocked DeepSeek, blocked ChatGPT for about a month in 2023, and in December 2024 it fined OpenAI 15 million euros.

Second, the law around a Chinese company is different.

In the US, companies can fight the government in court.

For example, Microsoft refused to hand over a customer's emails that were stored in Ireland, and that fight went all the way to the US Supreme Court in 2018.

China's Article 7 says companies "shall" cooperate with intelligence work and keep it secret, so a public fight like that is hard to picture.

Third, China does the same thing.

OpenAI doesn't offer ChatGPT in China, and in 2024 it also blocked API access from China. Google and Facebook have been blocked there for years.

*[optional line: And stay for this last one, because it changes what the bans actually cover.]*

Fourth, the bans are narrower than they sound.

DeepSeek released its model as open weights. That means anyone can download the model and run it on their own computers.

If you run it on your own server, your data doesn't go to China at all.

Even inside the Pentagon, staff could still use DeepSeek's model through an approved platform called Ask Sage, which doesn't connect to Chinese servers.

The one thing to watch is that the new October order also covers other companies' products "developed using DeepSeek implementations," and it doesn't define exactly what that means.

So if I was arguing for the bans, I'd say this. The US isn't stopping anyone from using the model. It's stopping government data from going to a company that has to cooperate with Chinese intelligence. And I think that's a reasonable thing for a government to want.

### The hypocrisy: America's own surveillance laws

So where do I think the hypocrisy is in the US banning Chinese AI?

The main argument against DeepSeek is that a Chinese company can be forced to give your data to the Chinese government.

Europe has been making that exact argument about American tech companies for years.

Remember the diary at your friend's house.

Now put the diary at an American friend's house.

The US has a law called FISA Section 702, from 2008.

It lets US intelligence agencies, with approval from a special court, make American companies hand over the communications of people who aren't American and are outside the US.

That's most of us watching from Nigeria.

*[on screen: FISA Section 702 / targets non-Americans outside the US / data held by US companies]*

In 2020, the European Union's top court looked at that law and struck down the deal that let companies move Europeans' data to America.

The court said US surveillance under laws like Section 702 wasn't limited to what's strictly necessary, and that Europeans had no proper way to challenge it in court.

Then there's the CLOUD Act, from 2018.

It says that American companies have to hand over data when they get a valid US legal order, even if that data is stored in another country.

And Microsoft has been asked about this directly.

In June 2025, Microsoft France's director of public and legal affairs, Anton Carniaux, sat in front of the French Senate.

They asked him if he could guarantee, under oath, that French citizens' data would never be sent to the US government without France agreeing.

He said, "No, I cannot guarantee that," and then added, "but, again, it has never happened before."

*[on screen: Anton Carniaux, Microsoft France, French Senate, June 2025: "No, I cannot guarantee that"]*

To be fair to the US, after the 2020 ruling it changed some rules, and in 2023 Europe and the US agreed a new data deal with a new review court.

This is how I see it.

When the US says it can't trust an app because a foreign government can reach the data, it's describing exactly what other countries say about American apps.

I believe the honest version of the US argument is "we don't trust China."

And that's a reasonable position for a government to take.

My problem is when it gets presented as a principle about protecting people's data, because the US doesn't hold its own companies to that principle when the data belongs to the rest of us.

### Free flow of data, and the TikTok deal

The second place I see hypocrisy in the US banning Chinese tech is in how it talks about data crossing borders.

For years, US trade policy pushed for data to flow freely between countries, and against rules that make companies store data at home. It wrote that into deals like the one with Mexico and Canada in 2019.

Then in October 2023, the US pulled its support for those same proposals at the World Trade Organization, saying it needed "policy space" to work out its own rules.

And since April 2025, a US Justice Department rule has restricted sending large amounts of Americans' sensitive data to China and five other countries.

Now, protecting your citizens' data is reasonable. Nigeria has a data protection law that does the same thing.

My problem is that the US spent years telling other countries that keeping data at home was a trade barrier, and now it does a version of it too.

Then there's TikTok.

In April 2024, the US passed a law saying TikTok had to be sold by its Chinese owner, ByteDance, or be banned in the US.

In January 2025, the Supreme Court said the law was allowed.

Then the President delayed enforcing it several times.

And in January 2026, it ended in a deal.

A new US company now runs TikTok in America, with Oracle, Silver Lake and MGX each holding 15%, and Oracle running the algorithm in its US cloud.

ByteDance kept nearly 20%.

*[on screen: TikTok law April 2024 / Supreme Court Jan 2025 / deal Jan 2026 / ByteDance keeps nearly 20%]*

People who support the deal say that was the point. Control of the app and the algorithm moved to the US.

But I think if TikTok was as dangerous as the law said, it's strange that it ended in a business deal where the company it was meant to remove still owns a share.

### Who gets to use AI: chips and export controls

The third place I see hypocrisy is in who the US lets use AI at all.

Since October 2022, the US has restricted selling advanced AI chips to China.

The US says it's about national security, mainly about China's military using American chips.

In January 2025, the US went further and published a rule that split the whole world into three groups for AI chips.

The US and 18 close partners had almost no limits.

China and countries under a US arms embargo were mostly blocked.

And everybody else, which included Nigeria, sat in the middle, with limits on how much computing power they could buy.

*[on screen: AI Diffusion Rule, Jan 2025 / group 1: US + 18 partners / group 3: China + arms-embargoed countries / group 2: everyone else, including Nigeria]*

That rule was cancelled in May 2025, before it took effect.

Then in December 2025, President Trump said Nvidia could sell its H200 chips to approved customers in China, as long as 25% went to the United States.

So chips that were a national security risk could be sold to China, if the US got a cut.

I think that tells you national security can be a bargaining position as well as a principle.

*[optional cut starts here: if you'd rather not include the Anthropic example, cut from here to OPTIONAL CUT END]*

And it isn't only chips.

In June 2026, the US Commerce Department sent Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, a directive that required a licence before any foreign person could use two of its newest models.

Anthropic said it couldn't block only foreign users at such short notice, so it switched those models off for everyone, everywhere.

The directive was lifted at the end of June.

I use Claude every day for work, so that one caught my attention.

*[optional cut ends here]*

So American AI can be cut off by the American government, for reasons that have nothing to do with you.

### What the US ban on Chinese AI means for Nigeria

So what does the US banning Chinese AI mean for countries like Nigeria?

We use American and Chinese tech side by side.

Huawei, a Chinese company, has been in Nigeria since 1999 and has become one of the biggest suppliers of our telecom networks.

In 2018, China's Export-Import Bank lent Nigeria 328 million dollars for a national internet project run by Galaxy Backbone, the government's own tech company, and Huawei worked on it.

And at the same time, most of us run our lives on Gmail, WhatsApp, Microsoft and ChatGPT.

And Chinese AI is already here.

In January 2026, a Microsoft report found that in several African countries, including Ethiopia, Zimbabwe, Uganda and Niger, DeepSeek had roughly 11 to 14 percent of the AI chatbot market.

Microsoft said being free had "lowered the barrier for millions of users."

So for us, the choice isn't a clean one.

Whichever app you use, your data probably leaves Nigeria, and it sits under another country's law. America and China both have laws that let their governments reach it.

Nigeria's Data Protection Act from 2023 already says personal data should only go to countries with adequate protection, and the regulator's guidance lists government access to the data as one of the things to check.

That's the same question, and I think it should be asked about American companies and Chinese companies the same way.

So this is what I would tell you.

If you work in government, or you handle client data, don't paste anything sensitive into any free chatbot, American or Chinese.

At my workplace, there's no rule about AI tools. We just use the ones the company uses. So if your workplace doesn't have a rule either, you have to be careful yourself.

Before you trust a tool with something important, ask whose law can reach that data, and ask it the same way for both countries.

If you build products with AI, remember that open models like DeepSeek's can run on servers you choose, and keep a backup provider, so one decision in Washington or Beijing doesn't switch off your product.

And I'd like Nigeria's own rules to hold American and Chinese companies to the same standard.

So tell me in the comments. Is the US right to ban DeepSeek on government devices, or is it hypocrisy?

ideas.script:
### Open

I saw a short TikTok about Kenya suing Meta, the company that owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.

And I didn't even know the gist, so I went digging.

I read the court rulings and the reporting.

And there isn't one case.

There are three big cases against Meta in Kenyan courts, plus a 2026 investigation by Kenya's data regulator, and most of the cases were brought by former workers and victims.

In this video, I'll take you through each one, what Meta says, and what it could mean for Nigeria and the rest of Africa.

### What content moderators do and why it happened in Nairobi

All the Kenya cases against Meta start with a job most people have never heard of. It's called content moderation.

When someone reports a post on Facebook, or a system flags it, very often a human being has to look at it and decide if it breaks the rules.

That means looking at the worst things people upload, every day, as your job.

That can be violent videos, abuse, or people hurting themselves.

Meta doesn't do most of this work with its own staff. It pays outsourcing companies to do it.

In Nairobi, one of those companies was Sama, an American outsourcing company with a big office in Kenya.

Sama's Nairobi office moderated Facebook content for the region until early 2023.

In February 2022, TIME magazine published an investigation by Billy Perrigo called "Inside Facebook's African Sweatshop."

It reported that some of the moderators were paid as little as $1.50 an hour.

*[on screen: TIME, Feb 2022 / "as little as $1.50 per hour"]*

Sama said it paid well above Kenya's minimum wage, and it said it was "completely inaccurate" to suggest people were hired under false pretenses.

One of the people in that story was Daniel Motaung, a moderator from South Africa.

He had tried to organise his colleagues to push for better pay and conditions, and he was fired in 2019.

Sama denies that it fired him for organising.

And in May 2022, he went to court.

### Case one, Daniel Motaung vs Sama and Meta

The first Kenyan case against Meta was filed in May 2022 by Daniel Motaung, a former Facebook content moderator from South Africa.

He sued Sama and Meta at the Employment and Labour Relations Court in Nairobi.

His case includes claims of human trafficking, because he says people were recruited without being told clearly what the job was.

It also says he was fired for trying to form a union, and that the work gave him post-traumatic stress disorder, which is PTSD, without enough mental health support.

These are his claims, and the court hasn't decided them yet.

Meta's first answer was that it shouldn't be in the case at all.

It argued that it's a foreign company that doesn't operate in Kenya, and that Sama employed him, not Meta.

In February 2023, the judge disagreed and ruled that Meta was a "proper party" to the case. That means Meta has to answer the claims, alongside Sama.

*[on screen: Feb 2023 / Meta is a "proper party" to the case]*

Amnesty International said that meant Meta would be "significantly subjected to a court of law in the global south" for the first time.

In February 2026, the court was supposed to give rulings in his case and in the moderators' case, and it postponed them.

As of October 2026, his case still hasn't been decided.

### Case two, the 185 Facebook moderators who lost their jobs

The biggest Kenyan case against Meta is about the Facebook content moderators who lost their jobs in 2023.

In January 2023, Sama announced it was leaving content moderation work, and around 200 moderators in Nairobi lost their jobs.

Meta moved the work to another outsourcing company, called Majorel.

In March 2023, 43 of the moderators went to court, and the group later grew to about 185.

Their lawyer is Mercy Mutemi, a Kenyan lawyer who now runs a group called The Oversight Lab Africa.

They say the layoffs were unlawful, and they say Meta told Majorel not to hire them, which they call blacklisting.

Again, those are their claims, and they haven't been tested at trial.

In 2023, the labour court ordered Sama to keep paying the moderators while the case went on, and ordered Meta to provide "proper medical, psychiatric and psychological care."

The Court of Appeal later set aside the part about working conditions, because it said the judge had made final orders at an early stage of the case, when he shouldn't have.

*[optional line: And then the case went all the way to the Court of Appeal, on the question of whether a Kenyan court can judge Meta at all.]*

On 20 September 2024, three judges of Kenya's Court of Appeal threw out Meta's appeal, and said the case can be heard in Kenya.

*[on screen: Court of Appeal, 20 Sept 2024 / Meta can be sued in Kenya]*

In December 2024, the moderators' lawyers filed medical reports with the court.

Dr Ian Kanyanya, the head of mental health services at Kenyatta National Hospital, assessed 144 of the former moderators, and 81% of them were classed as having severe PTSD.

Meta told CNN it takes the support of moderators seriously, and that its contracts with outsourcing companies set expectations on counselling, training and fair pay.

It didn't comment on the medical reports, because the case is still going on.

Since then, the case has moved slowly.

In April 2026, the court ordered a Meta director, Laura O'Hanlon, to come and be cross-examined about a sworn statement she gave for Meta.

That same month, one of the moderators told Capital FM, "To date, we have not been receiving any mental health care."

As of October 2026, the main case still hasn't been decided.

### Can you sue Meta in Kenya?

The biggest question in all the Kenya cases is whether a Kenyan court can judge Meta at all.

Lawyers call this jurisdiction. It means a court's power to hear a case.

Meta's answer has been no, again and again.

In the moderators' case, Meta argued that "There is no permissive law that allows this court to exercise jurisdiction" outside Kenya's borders.

It says it's registered in the United States and Ireland, it doesn't have staff in Kenya, and the moderators worked for Sama.

So let me give you an example to make it simple.

Imagine an estate in Lagos hires a security company to guard the gate.

The guards wear the security company's uniform, and the security company pays them.

But the estate decides their shifts, gives them the list of who to let in, checks their work every day, and one day tells the security company it doesn't need them anymore.

If those guards are treated badly, can they sue only the security company, or the estate too?

That's basically the question Kenyan courts have been answering about Meta and Sama.

*[on screen: the estate = Meta / the security company = Sama / the guards = the moderators]*

So far, Kenyan courts have said Meta can be part of these cases.

In 2023, the labour court treated Meta as the moderators' main employer for that stage of the case, partly because they worked on Meta's own systems.

In 2024, the Court of Appeal said the labour court was right to step in, because the layoffs were happening in Kenya and affecting people in Kenya.

One thing to be clear about, though.

These rulings only decide that the cases can be heard in Kenya.

Who is right, and whether Meta owes anybody anything, gets decided later, at trial.

### Case three, the Ethiopia hate speech case against Meta

The third Kenyan case against Meta is about Facebook's algorithm and the war in northern Ethiopia.

Abrham Meareg's father, Professor Meareg Amare Abrha, was a chemistry professor at Bahir Dar University in Ethiopia.

In 2021, during the war, Facebook posts shared his name and his photo, with false claims linking him to a rebel group, because he was Tigrayan.

Weeks later, he was killed by gunmen outside his home.

His son says he asked Facebook several times to take the posts down, and NPR reported that some were still up when he filed the case.

The second person bringing the case is Fisseha Tekle, a legal adviser at Amnesty International, who says his reports on the violence made him a target of online abuse.

The third is the Katiba Institute, a Kenyan rights organisation.

They filed in December 2022, at the High Court in Nairobi, because they say content from Ethiopia was being moderated from Meta's hub in Nairobi.

They're asking the court to make Meta change its algorithm so it stops promoting hate, hire enough moderators who speak the local languages, and set up a fund for victims.

When they filed, that fund was reported as about 1.6 billion US dollars.

*[on screen: what they're asking for / change the algorithm / more moderators who speak local languages / a fund for victims]*

Meta told NPR that "Hate speech and incitement to violence are against these rules, and we invest heavily in teams and technology" to find and remove that content.

Meta also argued that a Kenyan court can't hear this case, because it's governed by American law, and Facebook's terms say disputes go to US courts.

On 3 April 2025, Justice L. N. Mugambi of the High Court rejected that.

He wrote, "The issues raised are substantial and transcend the interests of the parties involved in the Petition."

And he sent the case to the Chief Justice to set up a bench of judges to hear it.

Abrham said afterwards, "Mark Zuckerberg may imagine that justice begins and ends at the US border."

Meta appealed that ruling.

Foxglove, a UK group that supports the case, says there was a hearing in Nairobi on 16 July 2026, and it expects a result in the coming months.

As of October 2026, I couldn't find a decision.

### Meta's smart glasses, Sama, and Kenya's data regulator

In 2026, Meta and Kenya were in the news again, and this time it was about Meta's smart glasses.

Ray-Ban Meta glasses have a camera and Meta's AI assistant built in.

In late February 2026, two Swedish newspapers, Svenska Dagbladet and Göteborgs-Posten, published interviews with workers at Sama in Nairobi who reviewed footage from the glasses.

The workers said that footage included people undressing, using the toilet and having sex.

A Meta spokesperson told TechCrunch that photos and videos stay on the user's device unless the user shares them.

He said that when content is shared with Meta AI, Meta "sometimes" uses contractors to review it, and that it filters the data to protect people's privacy.

In March, a Nairobi digital rights group called The Oversight Lab asked Kenya's Office of the Data Protection Commissioner, the ODPC, to investigate.

On 31 March 2026, the ODPC said it had opened an investigation into whether this follows Kenya's Data Protection Act.

*[on screen: ODPC investigation opened 31 March 2026]*

Then Meta ended its contract with Sama.

Meta said Sama "don't meet our standards." Sama said it was "surprised and disappointed."

On 16 April 2026, Sama gave redundancy notices to 1,108 workers in Nairobi.

So this investigation is the one part of the story where Kenya, the state, is looking into Meta.

As of October 2026, I couldn't find any published findings.

### Where the Kenyan government stands on Meta

If you only read the headline, you might think the Kenyan government is leading the fight against Meta. The real picture is more mixed.

Kenya wants outsourcing jobs, and President William Ruto has talked about making Kenya an outsourcing hub like India or the Philippines.

In December 2024, at a town hall in Nairobi, Ruto said Sama had come to him about its legal troubles.

And he said, "Now I can report to you that we have changed the law, so nobody will take you to court again on any matter."

*[on screen: President Ruto, Dec 2024 / "nobody will take you to court again on any matter"]*

TIME looked at the bill he meant and reported that its text would keep clients like Meta from being pulled into lawsuits against their Kenyan contractors.

Meta told TIME, "Meta has not advocated for changes to these laws."

Tech workers went to court to stop that bill, and in June 2026 the High Court declined to step in.

On 19 August 2026, Kenya's National Assembly passed the outsourcing changes.

According to an investigation by The Continent and Business Day published in September, they were waiting for the president's signature, and the report didn't give the final wording, so I'm not going to guess what it says.

*[optional line: Now put that next to the smart glasses investigation.]*

So through its data regulator, the government is investigating Meta, and through Parliament, it's changing the rules in a way that could protect outsourcing companies and their clients.

### What Kenya vs Meta means for Nigeria and Africa

So what does Kenya versus Meta mean for Nigeria and the rest of Africa?

First, the work moves.

After the Kenya layoffs, Foxglove said, drawing on reporting by The Guardian and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, that Meta's moderation for the region had moved to Accra in Ghana, through Majorel.

So whatever Kenyan courts decide about who is responsible could matter to workers in Ghana, or in Nigeria if this kind of work comes here.

A Kenyan ruling doesn't bind a Nigerian court.

But Nigeria and Kenya both use the common law system, and courts in common law countries sometimes look at each other's decisions when they're deciding something new.

Second, Nigeria has mostly gone after Meta through regulators.

In 2024, Nigeria's consumer protection commission, the FCCPC, fined Meta 220 million dollars over WhatsApp's data practices, and a tribunal upheld that fine in April 2025.

And in 2025, Nigeria's data protection commission ordered Meta to pay 32.8 million dollars, and later that year it settled with Meta out of court, which Premium Times reported set those orders aside.

So that's two different tools. In Kenya, it's mostly people taking Meta to court. In Nigeria, it's mostly regulators, and both take years.

I think if a company sets the rules of the job, the work happens on its systems, and it decides when the job ends, it should share responsibility for the people doing that job, whatever name is on their payslip.

The strongest argument on the other side is jobs.

If companies like Meta can be sued in Kenya over their contractors' workers, some might move the work to countries where they can't be, and Ruto said Sama had been planning to move to Uganda.

Meta has also said it requires its partners to provide "industry-leading pay, benefits and support."

And none of the workers' or victims' claims has been proven at trial yet.

So tell me in the comments, who do you think should be responsible for these workers, the outsourcing company, Meta, or both?

ideas.title: How Uber Serves Millions of Translations From Memory
ideas.format: TV / slide behind you with a flat engineering diagram (four boxes for one book, the garbage collector as a cleaner); Uber's engineering post as the receipt (screenshot as title, T9).
ideas.length: about 13:28 (2021 spoken words, at about 150 a minute).
ideas.hook: So there's this thing I read from Uber's engineering team, posted on the 15th of October, 2026.
ideas.summary: A simple explainer of Uber Engineering's post "Translations at Scale: Memory Optimization Techniques That Kept Uber's P99 Under 1ms" by Cristian Velazquez (15 October 2026). It covers what app translations are, why holding them in memory got expensive for Uber's Go services, the two fixes, the real numbers, and what a regular developer can take from it.

record.where: Desk with the laptop, a second screen or TV behind you for the diagrams.
record.how: Sitting, chest up, explaining-to-a-junior-dev energy. Read from the teleprompter, phone sideways (16:9) on a stand at eye level.
