ideas.script:
### Open

So there's this thing I read from Uber's engineering team, posted on the 15th of October, 2026.

Uber serves millions of translations per second, all from memory, and the library holding them had become one of the biggest users of memory across their Go services.

In this video, I'll explain why that got expensive, the two things Uber changed, and their real numbers, and you don't need to be a developer to follow.

### What app translations are, and why Uber keeps them in memory

First, what do we mean by translations in an app?

When you open an app in French, every button and every message is in French. The app doesn't have a separate copy of itself for every language.

Instead, every piece of text gets a name, called a key. And for every key, there's a version in each language.

Developers call this internationalisation, or i18n for short, because there are 18 letters between the i and the n.

Say we have a bookstore app, and we want to tell a customer their order has been placed.

*[on screen: code]*

```
// en
{ "order.placed": "Your order has been placed." }

// fr
{ "order.placed": "Votre commande a été passée." }
```

The code only asks for "order.placed", and the user gets it in their own language.

Uber's post describes a translation as a key and a language together.

So one key in ten languages is ten translations.

And in the service they use as their example, there were over 2 million translations.

*[on screen: "a translation is a <key>-<language> combination" (Uber Engineering)]*

Uber keeps all of them in memory. In their words, "To save costs and reduce latency, we serve all these translations from memory."

Memory here means the RAM of the server. Reading from RAM is very fast, much faster than asking another service over the network, or reading from a disk.

Think of a waiter who has the whole menu memorised, compared to one who walks to the back office every time you ask what's in a dish.

But memory isn't free, and when you run thousands of copies of a service, it adds up very quickly.

### Why holding translations in memory got expensive

So why did keeping translations in memory become a problem for Uber?

Most of the services involved here are written in Go, the programming language.

Go has something called a garbage collector.

While your program runs, it keeps creating small things in memory, called objects.

The garbage collector's job is to find the objects nobody is using anymore and free that memory, so you don't have to do it by hand.

Picture a cleaner in a warehouse. Every so often, they walk through and check every box to see if anyone still needs it.

If the warehouse has a few hundred boxes, that's quick.

If it has millions, the cleaner spends a lot of time walking around, and that time is CPU your servers are paying for.

*[on screen: more objects = more for the garbage collector to check = more CPU]*

Uber's post says garbage collection "continues to be a top consumer of compute for our Go services."

When they looked at memory profiles across their fleet, their translation library was, in their words, "one of the top contributors in terms of size and number of objects."

In one translation service, 70% of the objects came from translations, and over 20% of the service's CPU was going to garbage collection.

Uber had already tried tuning the garbage collector before. Back in 2021, the same author wrote about a tool they built called GOGCTuner.

But that kind of tuning works by letting the app use more of the memory it has. The post says it "does nothing when free memory is already low."

So this time, they had to change how the translations were stored.

### Fix one, fewer objects per translation

Uber's first fix for the translation library was to cut down the number of objects each translation created.

The translations were stored in something in Go called a sync.Map. It's a map that's safe to use from many parts of the program at the same time.

But the way sync.Map worked before Go 1.24, storing one translation created four separate objects in memory.

So it's like packing one book inside a box, inside another box, inside another box, inside another box.

With over 2 million translations, that's millions of boxes for the cleaner to check.

*[on screen: code]*

```
// before: four objects for every translation
var store sync.Map

// after: a plain map of strings, with one lock for the whole map
type Store struct {
    mu    sync.RWMutex
    items map[string]string
}
```

So they moved to a plain Go map of strings, with one lock in front of it.

That lock is called an RWMutex. Many readers can read at the same time, and when a writer needs to update the translations, it waits its turn.

For the service in their example, that one change gave them "over 30% improvement in CPU usage."

Over 30% from changing how a map stores things. That's a big win.

But the memory was still high, and that was the next problem.

### The second problem, 800MB of translations and a double copy

Even after fixing the objects, Uber's translations were still taking up a lot of memory.

The post explains why. They had cut down the pointers, but they were still storing the same amount of text.

For the service in their example, the translations came as a compressed JSON file of about 150 megabytes.

Once it was uncompressed and loaded into memory, it took about 800 megabytes.

*[on screen: 150MB compressed file, about 800MB in memory]*

And there was a second problem with refreshing.

Every couple of hours, the service loads a fresh copy of the translations.

It builds the new copy in the background, and when it's ready, it swaps it in for the old one in one step, so users never see half-loaded text.

But for up to a minute, the service is holding two full copies at once.

So 800 megabytes becomes about 1.6 gigabytes for that minute, and the post says that in some services, this caused them to run out of memory.

Then the team noticed something important. In their words, "the percentage of translations used was pretty low."

So they looked at their options.

One option was to move translations to a separate service and fetch them over the network. They said no, because of "higher costs due to overhead from network calls, higher latency, and higher chances of failures."

Another option was to give each service only the translations it needs. They said no to that too, because of the maintenance, like having to update a key in many repositories.

### Fix two, popular translations in memory, the rest on disk

Uber's second fix was a hybrid. In their words, "a small portion was in memory, everything else on disk."

Think of a bookshop. The books people ask for every day stay on the counter. Everything else goes to the store room, and the staff keep a small card that says exactly where each book is.

The rest of the code didn't have to change. It still calls the same Get and Put functions it always did.

*[on screen: Get() and Put() stay the same. Popular translations in memory, everything else on disk.]*

The small card works like this.

Every key stays in memory, but in a much smaller form. They run the key through a hash, which turns any text into a short fixed-size code, like a fingerprint. Uber uses 6 bytes.

The first byte picks one of 256 groups, called shards. Each shard has its own lock, its own entries in memory, and its own file on disk.

So instead of one big queue at one counter, you have 256 counters, and people spread out.

Now, a short fingerprint has a risk. Two different keys could end up with the same code. That's called a collision. It's like two people in a room sharing a birthday.

Uber did the maths for 10 million keys. With 6 bytes, the chance of even one collision was about 16%, and the expected number of collisions was less than one. With 5 bytes, they'd expect about 45.

So they chose 6 bytes, and for the rare key that collides, there's a fallback that uses the original key. The post says only a couple of keys hit that path.

*[on screen: 6-byte fingerprint per key. 256 shards. Collisions fall back to the original key.]*

The value next to each key is also tiny. 2 bytes say where the translation sits in memory, if it's there, and 3 bytes say where it sits in the file on disk.

So each entry is 11 bytes in total, no matter how long the translation is.

Then they had to decide which translations stay in memory. For that, they used something called an LRU, which means least recently used.

It's like a small fridge. When it's full, the thing you haven't touched in the longest time is the one that comes out.

Updating that list on every single read would cost too much, so they only save the last time each entry was used.

And this is a small detail I love. When they profiled it, just checking the time was adding 3 to 5% extra CPU.

So they have one background task that keeps the current time in a shared value, and everyone reads from that.

Like one big clock on the office wall, so nobody has to keep checking their phone.

*[optional line: And the refresh problem from earlier gets fixed here too.]*

When the translations refresh every couple of hours, they only preload the entries that were used in the last 15 minutes.

Before they did that, the share of reads served from memory dropped every time a refresh happened, and disk reads went up. Preloading the recent ones fixed that.

### The results, with Uber's real numbers

So what did Uber's translation changes actually achieve? These numbers are all from their post.

At startup, the translation store now sits at about 40 megabytes, which is only the keys and the small cards. Before, it was about 800. That's an over 90% improvement.

They capped memory at 50,000 translations, which usually keeps it between 80 and 120 megabytes.

A refresh now needs about 40 megabytes extra, instead of a second full copy.

*[on screen: about 800MB before. About 40MB at startup. Usually 80 to 120MB with a 50,000 cap.]*

In the service they show at the end, about 30,000 out of more than 4 million entries are in memory. That's about 1%.

And over 99.9% of reads are still answered from memory.

For the less than 0.1% that have to go to disk, the p99 is under 100 microseconds.

p99 means 99 out of every 100 of those reads are faster than that. And a microsecond is a millionth of a second.

Overall, that service's memory went from about 2.7 gigabytes to about 750 megabytes.

*[on screen: about 1% in memory. Over 99.9% served from memory. Memory 2.7GB to 750MB.]*

The post ends by saying, "Due to our scale, having unoptimized in-memory cache solutions across thousands of instances gets expensive." They're now looking at other caches that use a lot of memory, and they might build a general version of this.

The post also thanks Uber's Internationalization team, who helped with the reviews and the rollout.

### What you can take from Uber's translations fix for your own app

So what can you take from Uber's translations story if your app is nowhere near Uber's size?

To be honest, most apps will never have this exact problem. A bookstore app in English and French might have a few hundred strings.

If you're using Laravel, for example, your translations live in a lang folder.

*[on screen: code]*

```
// lang/en/orders.php
return [
    'placed' => 'Your order has been placed.',
];

// in your code
echo __('orders.placed');
```

Laravel already loads translations lazily. The orders file for French is only read the first time a request asks for something in it, and then it's kept for the rest of that request.

With the usual PHP setup, every request starts fresh, so that memory is gone when the request ends.

One thing I found in Laravel's code. If you also keep a JSON file for a language, like lang/fr.json, the first translation in that language loads the whole JSON file.

So if that one file grows to thousands of lines, you're loading all of them to show one sentence.

And queue workers are different. Laravel's docs say they're long-lived processes that keep the app in memory. So what one job loads can still be there for the next job.

So the lessons I'm taking from Uber are simple ones.

Measure first. Uber didn't guess. They looked at memory profiles and saw the translation library near the top. In PHP, even memory_get_peak_usage() will tell you how much a request used.

Then ask how much of what you load is actually used. Uber found most of their translations were barely touched, and that changed the whole design.

And Uber's own two lessons from the post are, "Create the smallest possible amount of references," because that's less work for the garbage collector, and "Keep an eye on the total memory consumed and how often those objects are truly used."

So, what's something your app loads on every request that it might not need? Tell me in the comments.

ideas.hook: I read almost every day.
ideas.summary: A warm, personal video built on your own dictation. You read almost every day with a full-time job and a full master's, including books you don't have to read, and this is how: you use reading to replace something, you read while you eat, there's always a book in your bag, and you read what you enjoy.

record.where: Several places, one day: your desk, the dining table at lunch, the tram or bus, your bag at the door.

ideas.script:
### Open

I read almost every day.

I have a full-time job, and I'm doing a full master's degree.

And I still read books that I'm not mandated to read.

By books that I'm not mandated to read, I mean non-academic books.

Of course, I'm doing a master's degree, so I have to read the books that pertain to my program.

But I also read books outside of that. Books that won't hurt me if I don't read them, but I still read them anyway.

I think I read a lot, so I have a lot of opinions about reading.

So in this video, I'll tell you how I read every day, what I've been reading this year, and what the research says about reading fiction.

### I use reading to replace doomscrolling

So how do you read every day when you have a full-time job and a master's?

How do you read like that?

I think for me, you have to use it to replace something.

Most of us don't have an empty hour sitting around, waiting for a book.

For me, one thing I always do is use books to replace doomscrolling. That's like my one thing.

And I'll be honest, I'm not a heavy doomscroller. My screen time is already low for an average person.

But I want it lower, because I don't see the benefit.

So the time I would have spent scrolling, I spend reading.

And there's research on swapping one thing for another like this.

The psychologist Peter Gollwitzer calls it an implementation intention. In plain words, it's an if-then plan.

You decide ahead of time, "if this happens, then I'll do that."

For example, "if I reach for my phone to scroll, then I'll open my book."

In 2006, Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran combined 94 tests of these plans.

On average, making an if-then plan had a medium-to-large effect on whether people reached their goals.

*[on screen: if-then plans, 94 tests combined: a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals. Gollwitzer and Sheeran, 2006]*

Then in 2011, Marieke Adriaanse, Gollwitzer and their colleagues tested plans that replace a habit with something else.

The plan took away the old habit's head start. When the moment came, the old habit no longer came to mind faster than the new thing.

But the new thing didn't become automatic straight away. It only won when people really wanted it.

So the book you swap in has to be one you actually want to read.

If you want more ideas for what to do instead of doomscrolling, I made a whole video on that, and I'll link it.

### I read while I eat

Another way I read every day is while I'm eating.

If I'm eating, instead of watching a movie or doing something else, I read.

Think about how many times you eat in a day.

That's two or three small windows, every single day, and they add up.

If you read 20 pages a day, that's 7,300 pages in a year.

If a book is about 300 pages, that's about 24 books.

*[on screen: 20 pages a day x 365 days = 7,300 pages = about 24 books of 300 pages]*

You don't need a free afternoon to be a reader.

The time you already spend eating is enough to start.

### There is always a book in my bag

Another thing that helps me read every day is that I take books out.

I love to take books out with me.

If you jam me anywhere, there's nowhere you jam me and you will not see a book in my bag.

There is always a book in my bag.

So when I'm waiting on something, I pick up my book, instead of my phone.

I think if your book is at home and your phone is in your pocket, the phone is going to win most of the time.

So put the book where your hand already goes.

### Read the books you enjoy

If you want to read every day, read the books that you enjoy.

And what I enjoy has changed this year.

I love reading the kind of books that people would call self-help books.

But since I started my master's program, I've noticed that I've been reading a lot less of the quote-unquote serious books.

I've been doing that less over the past year, I'm not gonna lie, because I'm in school and I'm doing a lot of school reading.

So most of my reading this year has really been fiction.

And I have also started to enjoy fiction, and started to really like fiction.

One of the writers I've found recently is Khaled Hosseini.

Oh my goodness, I love Khaled Hosseini so much.

If you don't know him, he's an Afghan-American novelist.

And I think enjoying it is what makes the reading happen every day.

If you only pick books because you feel you should, it's hard to keep picking them up.

### Is reading fiction productive?

When people ask how to read every day, I would say, of course you want to read something that is productive for you.

A lot of people think of fiction as something that is not so productive.

I don't think so.

I've always liked fiction, even though there was a season of my life where I read way less fiction.

And there's research on this, so I want to be careful here.

In 2013, David Kidd and Emanuele Castano published a study in the journal Science.

People read a short piece of literary fiction, or nonfiction, or popular fiction, or nothing at all.

Then they took tests of something called theory of mind.

Theory of mind is your ability to understand what other people are thinking and feeling.

One of the tests shows you photos of just the eyes of different people, and you pick the emotion you think they're feeling.

The people who read literary fiction did better, and the study got a lot of attention.

*[on screen: a short piece of literary fiction, then a theory of mind test. Kidd and Castano, Science, 2013]*

But when other researchers tried to repeat it, it didn't hold up well.

In 2016, Maria Eugenia Panero and her colleagues ran it again across three labs, with 792 people, and reading one short passage made no difference.

And in 2018, a big project led by Colin Camerer repeated 21 social science experiments from Nature and Science. This was one of the ones that didn't replicate.

So I won't tell you that one chapter of a novel makes you more empathetic.

But in that 2016 study, there was one thing that did show up. People who had read more fiction over their lives did better on the eyes test.

And when researchers put many studies together, they find a small effect.

In 2017, Micah Mumper and Richard Gerrig combined studies on people's reading over their lives. People who read more fiction tended to score a bit higher on empathy and theory of mind, and the link was small.

In 2018, David Dodell-Feder and Diana Tamir combined 14 experiments, and reading fiction had a small positive effect on understanding other people, compared with reading nonfiction or nothing.

*[on screen: one short passage, no clear effect / years of fiction reading, a small link. Panero et al. 2016; Mumper and Gerrig 2017; Dodell-Feder and Tamir 2018]*

So the honest answer is that the effect is small, and scientists are still working out how it works.

I read Khaled Hosseini's books because I love them, and if they help me understand people a little better, that's a bonus.

*[optional line: "And the last thing I want to say is the opinion I hold most strongly about reading."]*

### Just read

Apart from the kind of reading, how do you even read at all, any day?

Because one of the opinions I hold now is that you should just read, honestly.

You don't even have to be like, oh, I'm reading fiction, or I want to read self-help.

Just freaking read, literally.

It's just like, how do you not read every day?

And reading books has some interesting research behind it.

In 2016, Avni Bavishi, Martin Slade and Becca Levy at Yale looked at 3,635 people in the US, all aged 50 or older, for up to 12 years.

After they accounted for things like age, education, health and wealth, the people who read books had about a 20% lower risk of dying during those years than people who didn't read.

*[on screen: book readers, about 20% lower risk of dying over up to 12 years. Bavishi, Slade and Levy, Social Science and Medicine, 2016]*

It's an observational study, so it can't prove that reading caused it.

But I'll take it.

And I say almost every day, because some days it doesn't happen.

In 2010, Phillippa Lally and her team at University College London followed people trying to build a new daily habit.

For the people whose data they could track well, it took 66 days in the middle, and anywhere from 18 to 254 days, before the habit felt automatic.

And missing one day didn't really change how the habit formed.

*[on screen: a new habit took 18 to 254 days, 66 in the middle. Missing one day didn't really matter. Lally et al., 2010]*

So if you miss a day, pick the book up again the next day.

What are you reading right now? Tell me in the comments. I'd love to know.

ideas.script:
### Open

A video called "One Habit to Instantly Improve Reading Comprehension", by a YouTube channel called Closed Stacks, went viral and landed on my feed.

And when I watched it, my first thought was, for us, it might not just be one habit. It might be several habits.

I read almost every day, and as a master's student, a lot of what I read is stuff I have to understand.

So in this video, I'll go through six habits that research says help you understand and remember what you read, starting with the one from that video.

### Habit 1, preview before you read

The first habit that improves reading comprehension is to preview what you're about to read, before you read it.

This is the habit from the Closed Stacks video, and researchers call it schema activation.

A schema is the bundle of things you already know about something.

If I say "restaurant", you already know you'll sit down, get a menu, order, eat, and pay at the end.

When you read, your brain uses what you already know to make sense of the new thing.

There's a famous study from 1972 that shows how much this matters, and Closed Stacks cites it too.

John Bransford and Marcia Johnson had people listen to a short passage and then try to remember it.

The passage starts by saying the procedure is quite simple, and first you arrange things into different groups.

It goes on like that the whole way, and it never says what the procedure is.

Some people were told the topic before they heard it, which was washing clothes.

Some were told the topic after they heard it, and some were never told.

The people who knew the topic before understood the passage and remembered a lot more of it.

The people who were told the topic after didn't get that benefit.

*[on screen: told "washing clothes" before / it makes sense, they remember more · told after, or never / it doesn't]*

Everyone heard the same words.

The only difference was whether they knew it was about laundry while they were listening.

So how do you do this with a real book or chapter?

Before you start a chapter, spend a couple of minutes on the headings, the pictures or diagrams, and the summary at the end if there is one.

Then ask yourself, what do I already know about this topic?

Say you're about to read a chapter on how vaccines work.

You might remember that a vaccine trains your body to recognise a germ before you get sick.

That's your starting point, and the chapter hangs new details onto it.

For a novel, it can be as small as reading the back cover and thinking about where and when the story is set.

There's one warning, and Closed Stacks talks about this too.

Their video is about how schema activation can help your reading, and also how it can distort it.

If you switch on the wrong idea, it can pull your understanding in the wrong direction.

For example, if you see an article called "Python" and you assume it's about the programming language, the paragraphs about snakes will confuse you, because you'll keep trying to fit them into code.

So treat your preview as a guess, and when the text tells you something different, let the text win.

### Why rereading feels like it works

A lot of us try to improve our reading comprehension by rereading.

You read the chapter, you didn't get all of it, so you read it again.

In 2009, Jeffrey Karpicke, Andrew Butler and Henry Roediger asked 177 university students in the US how they study.

84% said they reread their notes or their textbook, and 55% said rereading was their number one strategy.

Only about 11% mentioned testing themselves, and only 1% said that was their main strategy.

*[on screen: 177 students · 84% reread · 55% said rereading was their #1 strategy · 11% tested themselves · 1% said testing was their #1]*

Rereading feels good because the second time, everything looks familiar.

The words flow, you recognise the examples, and that feeling makes you think you know it.

But recognising something when it's in front of you is a lot easier than pulling it out of your head when the book is closed.

In 2013, John Dunlosky and four other researchers reviewed ten popular study techniques and rated how useful each one is, based on the evidence.

Two got a high rating. Practice testing, which means quizzing yourself, and distributed practice, which means spreading your study out over time.

Three got a moderate rating. Elaborative interrogation, self-explanation, and interleaved practice.

And five got a low rating. Summarisation, highlighting, the keyword mnemonic, using mental images for text, and rereading.

*[on screen: Dunlosky et al., 2013 · HIGH: practice testing, distributed practice · MODERATE: elaborative interrogation, self-explanation, interleaved practice · LOW: summarisation, highlighting, keyword mnemonic, imagery for text, rereading]*

A low rating means the benefits they found were small, or didn't show up consistently, so rereading can still help a little.

But the authors suggest that students would get more from their time by swapping some of that rereading for testing themselves.

So the next habit is that swap.

### Habit 2, close the book and recall

The second habit that improves reading comprehension is to close the book and try to recall what you just read.

Researchers call this retrieval practice, and in Dunlosky's review, it's the practice testing that got the high rating.

In 2006, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke gave students a short science passage to learn.

One group studied it four times.

Another group studied it once, and then took three recall tests, where they wrote down everything they could remember, with no feedback.

Five minutes later, the group that studied four times remembered more. 83% of the ideas, against 71%.

But one week later, it flipped.

The group that studied four times remembered 40%, and the group that kept recalling remembered 61%.

*[on screen: studied 4 times / 83% after 5 min · 40% after 1 week · studied once, recalled 3 times / 71% after 5 min · 61% after 1 week (Roediger and Karpicke, 2006)]*

And when the researchers asked people to predict how well they'd remember it in a week, the group that studied four times was the most confident.

So the method that felt the best did the worst a week later.

So this is how you can do it with a book.

When you finish a chapter, or even a few pages, close it, and say or write down what you remember.

No peeking.

You'll find the gaps straight away.

Maybe you remember there were three causes of something, and you can only name two.

Then open the book, check, and fill the gap.

It will feel harder than rereading, and that's normal.

Researchers think the effort of pulling it out of your head is part of what makes it stay.

*[optional line: And this next part is the one I like the most, because it works for novels too.]*

If you come back the next day and recall it again, you're also doing the other high-rated technique, spreading your study out over time.

And for a novel, you can do a softer version.

Before you start reading today, try to remember what happened in the last chapter, before you open the book.

### Habit 3, ask why while you read

The third habit that improves reading comprehension is to keep asking "why" while you read, and to explain things to yourself.

Dunlosky's review covers two techniques here, and both got a moderate rating.

The first one is elaborative interrogation.

It's a long name for asking yourself why a fact is true.

Say you read that plants grow towards the light.

You stop and ask, why would that be?

Because plants need light to make their food, so growing towards it helps them survive.

Now that fact is connected to something you already know, and it's easier to understand and remember.

The second one is self-explanation.

You stop after a sentence or a paragraph and explain to yourself what it means, and how it connects to what you read before it.

In a 1994 study, Michelene Chi and her colleagues had eighth graders read a text about the circulatory system, which is how blood moves around your body.

One group was asked to explain each line to themselves, out loud.

The other group read the text twice.

The group that explained learned more, and within that group, the students who explained more understood more.

*[on screen: explain each line to yourself / learned more · read it twice / learned less (Chi et al., 1994)]*

So explaining it once did better than reading it twice.

And this is explaining it to yourself, while you read.

Explaining what you read to someone else is harder, and I made a separate video on why.

### Habit 4, slow down when the text gets hard

The fourth habit that improves reading comprehension is to slow down when the text gets hard, and to let yourself go back.

There are apps and courses that promise to teach you to read thousands of words a minute.

In 2016, Keith Rayner and four other researchers reviewed the science of how we read, and whether speed reading works.

They found that skilled readers average about 200 to 400 words a minute.

And they found a trade-off between speed and accuracy.

When people read faster, they understand less.

*[on screen: skilled readers / about 200 to 400 words a minute · read faster, understand less (Rayner et al., 2016)]*

Going back is also part of normal reading.

About 10 to 15% of the time, our eyes jump back to words we've already read.

In a 2014 study, Elizabeth Schotter, Randy Tran and Keith Rayner hid each word after people read it, so they couldn't look back.

Those readers understood less, and that was true for hard sentences and simple ones.

So if one sentence confuses you, going back to read it again is fine.

That's different from rereading the whole chapter as your way of studying.

Skimming is fine when you only want the gist, but for a chapter you need to understand, read at your normal pace, or slower.

### Habit 5, summarise in your own words

The fifth habit that improves reading comprehension is to summarise what you read in your own words, and I have to be honest about this one.

In Dunlosky's review, summarisation got a low rating.

The authors said many learners, including children, high school students and even some undergraduates, would need a lot of training to summarise well.

And the results across studies were mixed.

A summary that copies sentences from the book doesn't do much, because you're moving words from one page to another.

So if you're going to summarise, I would do it like this.

Close the book first, so the summary comes out of your head. That way, it's also retrieval practice.

Keep it short, for example three sentences for a whole chapter, so you have to pick the main ideas.

Use your own words. If I can only say it in the author's words, I take that as a sign I haven't understood that part yet.

Then open the book and check your summary against it.

*[on screen: close the book · three sentences · your own words · check it]*

This is my own suggestion, built from what the review found, so I'm not claiming anyone tested this exact method.

It takes the low-rated technique and makes it work with the high-rated one.

### Habit 6, read hard texts on paper when you can

The sixth habit that improves reading comprehension is about whether you read on paper or on a screen.

In 2018, Pablo Delgado and three colleagues combined 54 studies, with over 171,000 participants, published between 2000 and 2017.

On average, people understood a bit more when they read on paper than when they read on a screen.

The difference was small, but it showed up in both kinds of study designs they looked at.

There are three details in that study that tell you when this matters.

First, the paper advantage was bigger when people had a time limit.

When people read at their own pace, it was much smaller.

Second, it showed up for informational texts, like textbooks and articles.

For narrative texts, like stories, they found no difference, though they said only a few studies used stories.

This year, I've mostly been reading fiction, and I love Khaled Hosseini, so for novels, I don't think the format matters much.

Third, the paper advantage got bigger over the years they looked at, from 2000 to 2017.

*[on screen: paper vs screen (Delgado et al., 2018) · small advantage for paper · bigger with a time limit · informational texts, not stories · grew from 2000 to 2017]*

A later review from the same research group, published in 2024, looked at tablets and e-readers, and found an even smaller advantage for paper.

Researchers aren't fully sure why paper helps.

One idea they discuss is that we're used to skimming on screens, so we bring that habit with us when we read something serious.

So if the text is hard and informational, and you have the choice, I think paper is a good bet.

And if you're reading a novel on your phone on the bus, keep reading.

So tell me in the comments, which of these six habits do you already do, and which one are you going to try this week?

ideas.script:
### Open

You finish a book, and you enjoyed it. You even underlined things.

Then somebody asks you, "What is it about?"

And all you can say is, "It's really good, you should read it."

In an older video, I described this as being left with a feeling about the book rather than the book itself.

So in this video, I'll show you why that happens, with the research behind it, and what you can do after you close a book so you can actually explain it.

### Why you feel like you understood a book

That feeling of understanding a book you can't explain has a name. It's called the illusion of explanatory depth.

It comes from a 2002 study by two researchers at Yale, Leonid Rozenblit and Frank Keil.

They asked people how well they understood everyday things, like a zip, a flush toilet or a lock, on a scale from one to seven.

Then they asked them to write out, step by step, how the thing actually works.

Then they asked them a harder, more specific question about it.

After each step, people rated their understanding again, and the ratings kept dropping.

Frank Keil later wrote that the drop often came with "shock and surprise."

*[on screen: rate it, explain it, rate it again / the rating drops]*

So before you try to explain something, it feels like you know it, and when you try, the gaps show up.

The finding that matters most for reading is this one.

The researchers found that the illusion was much stronger for explanations, meaning how and why something works, than for other kinds of knowledge, like facts, procedures or stories.

So if you just finished a novel, you can usually tell someone what happened.

But a lot of non-fiction books are explanations.

A book about habits explains why you do what you do. A book about money explains how interest grows.

And explanations are exactly the kind of knowledge where your brain tells you that you understand more than you do.

### Why rereading feels like learning

When we can't explain a book, a lot of us try to fix it by reading it again, or by going back over our highlights.

In 2009, Jeffrey Karpicke, Andrew Butler and Henry Roediger asked 177 university students how they study.

About 84% said they reread their notes or textbooks, and about 55% said rereading was their number one strategy.

Only about one in ten mentioned practising recall, which means testing yourself.

*[on screen: ~84% reread / ~55% said it's their #1 strategy / ~1 in 10 practise recall]*

Rereading feels good, because the second time, the words come easier. You know what's coming next.

Psychologists call that ease fluency.

And your brain takes that ease as a sign that you've learned the thing, even when you haven't.

There's a study that shows how far this feeling can mislead you.

In 2006, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke gave students a short science passage, about the sun or about sea otters.

One group read the passage four times.

Another group read it once, and then wrote down everything they could remember, three times.

Before they left, students predicted how well they'd remember it a week later, and the group that read it four times was the most confident.

If you tested them five minutes later, the rereaders were actually ahead.

But a week later, the group that read it four times remembered about 40% of the passage, and the group that read it once and recalled it three times remembered about 61%.

*[on screen: read it 4 times, 40% after a week / read once + recalled 3 times, 61% after a week]*

So the group that felt the most ready remembered the least.

### Recognition vs recall

Your memory can do two different things with a book. It can recognise, and it can recall.

Recognising is when you see something and know you've seen it before.

Recalling is pulling it out of your head with nothing in front of you.

You know when you see someone at church or at the market, you know their face, but you can't remember their name?

Knowing the face is recognition. Remembering the name is recall.

In 2015, Adam Blake, Meenely Nazarian and Alan Castel at UCLA asked 85 students to draw the Apple logo from memory.

Most of them used Apple products.

Only one person drew it correctly.

Then they showed the students the real logo mixed in with versions that had small changes, and fewer than half picked the real one.

*[on screen: 85 students / 1 drew it correctly / fewer than half picked the real one]*

Every device I own is Apple, and I'm not sure I would have got it right either.

Alan Castel said, "People's memory, even for extremely common objects, is much poorer than they believe it to be."

So think about what happens when you reread a book.

The book is right there in front of you, so you only need recognition. Every sentence makes you go, "Yes, I know this."

When someone asks you to explain the book, there's no book. That's recall.

And if all you ever did was reread, you never practised recall.

### Close the book and write what you remember

The first thing you can do so you can explain what you read is to close the book and write down what you remember.

This is called retrieval practice, which means pulling things out of your memory on purpose, like the group in the sea otter study did.

After a chapter, close the book, open a blank page or your notes app, and write what the chapter said in your own words. No peeking.

Then open the book again and check.

What did you miss? What did you get wrong?

Those gaps are exactly the parts you would have stumbled on when someone asked you about the book.

It will feel harder than rereading, and that's normal.

You might be thinking, I already write summaries.

In 2013, John Dunlosky and his colleagues reviewed ten common study techniques. They rated summarising, rereading and highlighting as low usefulness, and testing yourself as high.

So I would write my summary with the book closed, because then the summary becomes a way of testing yourself.

And when you finish the whole book, try one more thing.

Mortimer Adler and Charles Van Doren, in How to Read a Book, have a rule for this. "State the unity of the whole book in a single sentence, or at most a few sentences."

So in one or two sentences, what is the whole book about?

If you can't do that yet, you know where to go back to.

By the way, I have an older video on reading the structure of a book before you start, which is for before you read. This part is for after you close the book.

### Explain it to someone without the book

The second thing you can do so you can explain what you read is to explain it to another person.

A lot of people call this the Feynman technique, after the physicist Richard Feynman, who was famous for explaining hard physics in simple words.

As far as I can find, Feynman never wrote it down as a technique himself. Other people wrote up the steps later.

The steps usually go like this. Pick the idea, explain it in simple words like you're talking to a beginner, notice where you get stuck, go back to the book, and try again.

The idea comes from stories like this one.

David Goodstein, a physicist at Caltech, wrote that he once asked Feynman to explain a hard idea in physics.

Feynman said he would prepare a lecture on it for first-year university students.

A few days later, he came back and said, "I couldn't do it. I couldn't reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don't really understand it."

*[on screen: "I couldn't reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don't really understand it." / Feynman, as told by David Goodstein]*

I used to run an after-school tutorial centre, and I loved teaching.

When you teach children, they keep asking why, and every why takes you one step deeper, until you reach a step you can't explain.

*[optional line: And there's a study that shows the one thing that makes explaining work.]*

In 2018, Aloysius Koh, Sze Chi Lee and Stephen Lim, researchers in Singapore, gave 124 students a text about the Doppler effect to study for ten minutes.

Then one group taught it to a camera with no notes.

Another group taught it by reading out a prepared script.

Another group wrote down everything they could remember, and the last group did maths problems.

A week later, they all took a surprise test.

The group that taught without notes and the group that wrote from memory did about the same, and both did better than the script group and the maths group.

The researchers concluded that the benefit of teaching came from the recall.

That's why I'd say, explain it without the book in your hand.

There's also something researchers at Stanford called the protégé effect. In their 2009 study, school children put more effort into learning when they were teaching a computer character than when they were learning for themselves.

And if you don't have anyone to explain it to, record a voice note to yourself and listen back.

### When you understand it but still can't explain it

Sometimes you do understand a book, and you still explain it badly. That has a name too. It's called the curse of knowledge.

The curse of knowledge is when you know something so well that you can't imagine what it's like to not know it.

I first saw the next example in a Closed Stacks video called "Why You Can't Explain What You Read," and Chip and Dan Heath made it famous in their book Made to Stick.

In 1990, a Stanford student called Elizabeth Newton ran an experiment for her PhD.

One person, the tapper, tapped out a well-known song like "Happy Birthday" on a table.

Another person, the listener, had to guess the song.

The tappers predicted that listeners would get it about half the time.

Across 120 songs, listeners got three.

*[on screen: tappers predicted ~50% / listeners got 3 out of 120 (2.5%)]*

When you tap, you hear the song in your head. The listener only hears knocking.

When you finish a book, you're the tapper.

You skip steps because they feel obvious to you, and the person listening only hears knocking.

So explain the book to someone who hasn't read it, and watch their face.

If your friend looks lost, that shows you which step you skipped.

Making videos is the same test for me. Before I can explain something to you on camera, I have to be able to explain it.

### Sometimes the problem is the book

Sometimes you can't explain a book because the writer didn't explain it well.

Closed Stacks goes into this in more detail, and I want to give you one study on it.

In 2006, Daniel Oppenheimer, a psychologist at Princeton, made versions of the same pieces of writing with more complicated words and with simpler ones.

People rated the writers of the complicated versions as less intelligent.

The paper won an Ig Nobel Prize, and its title is "Consequences of Erudite Vernacular Utilized Irrespective of Necessity," which I think is the joke.

*[on screen: "Consequences of Erudite Vernacular Utilized Irrespective of Necessity" / meaning: using long words when you don't need to]*

To be fair, some ideas are hard, and a book that takes effort isn't automatically badly written.

So this is what I would do.

If you've written down what you remember, explained it to someone, gone back to the page, and the same paragraph still makes no sense, I think it might be the writing.

Find another book or article on the same topic, because someone else might explain it better.

So tell me in the comments, what's a book you loved but couldn't explain when someone asked? Try explaining it to me in two sentences.

### Open

So basically, this whole video is about how I'm preparing for 2027 in terms of productivity.

I'm really excited for the year 2027.

There are so many things I'm putting in place for the year 2027, and literally, let's just talk about 2027 in terms of productivity.

And I want us to do this together.

By the end of this video, you'll have a simple end-of-year reset you can sit down and do for your own 2027, with the research behind each step.

### Why productivity is such a big deal to me

For me, productivity has been a topic that has been a really, really, really big deal in my life for the past few years.

Of course, I've always known what the word productivity means.

I didn't always think of it intentionally, but I've always lived life trying to live a productive life.

And I mean productive in the ways that I define productivity.

I don't think productive is just doing your nine to five or your job well.

I think there are so many areas of your life where you should be productive and you can be productive.

I remember my first serious encounter with productivity, when I first started to realise that it was a big deal.

I think it was about four years ago.

I experienced burnout that year, and one thing led to another, and I had a productivity coach.

And it really, really changed things for me.

Ever since that time, productivity has become something that I'm so conscious of in my day to day.

And I think that a lot of people do not think of productivity that consciously.

I don't know what is waiting for me in 2027.

I was telling someone the other day that there's just something about 2027 that is keeping me so excited.

So if you're also thinking about next year, sit with me, and let's get ready for it properly.

### Why the end of the year feels like a fresh start

A lot of us feel a pull to start again when a new year is coming, and there's research on why that happens.

In 2014, three researchers, Hengchen Dai, Katherine Milkman and Jason Riis, published a paper called "The Fresh Start Effect."

They looked at three kinds of real-world data.

First, they looked at Google searches for the word "diet" in the US.

Then they looked at how often students at one American university went to the gym.

And then they looked at goals people committed to on a goal-setting website called stickK.

All three went up right after what they called temporal landmarks.

A temporal landmark is a date that feels like a line in your calendar.

The start of a new year is one, and so is a new month, a new week, a new semester, your birthday, or the first day back after a holiday.

*[on screen: temporal landmarks / new year / new month / new week / new semester / birthday / after a holiday]*

For the "diet" searches, the biggest jump came at the start of a new year.

The researchers' explanation is that these dates help us put our old mistakes in an old chapter, and look at our lives from a bigger picture.

That part is their best explanation, and the paper didn't test it directly.

So if December makes you want to sit down and plan, that feeling is normal, and you can use it.

But you don't have to wait for the first of January.

The start of a new week and a new month showed the same pattern in their data, so any Monday can be your start.

And a fresh start gives you a push at the beginning, so the rest of this video is about what carries you after the push.

### Step 1, look back at 2026 by area of your life

The first step of an end-of-year reset is to look back at your year, one area of your life at a time.

I start here because of how I define productivity.

For me, being productive is bigger than doing your nine to five well.

There are so many areas of your life where you can be productive.

So take a page, and write those areas down.

For example, your work, your studies if you're in school, your health and your rest, your relationships, your money, your faith if that's part of your life, and the things you do because you love them.

*[on screen: a page with the areas written down the side / work / studies / health and rest / relationships / money / faith / things I love]*

Under each area, answer two questions.

What went well this year, and what drained me?

Then ask one more question for each area.

What did I keep saying yes to that I don't want to carry into next year?

For example, under work, you might write that you finished a project you're proud of.

And under rest, you might write that you worked most weekends.

Be honest with yourself, because nobody else is going to read this page.

When you're done, circle the one or two areas that need the most attention next year.

You don't have to fix every area of your life in one year.

### Check for burnout before you plan more

Before you add new goals for 2027, it helps to check how tired you already are.

About four years ago, I experienced burnout.

That's how I ended up with a productivity coach, and it's a big part of why I think about productivity the way I do now.

So I want to tell you what burnout means, because a lot of us use the word loosely.

The World Health Organization describes burnout in its classification of diseases, which is called ICD-11.

It says burnout is a syndrome that comes from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed.

Chronic here means it's been going on for a long time.

The WHO describes three signs.

The first one is feeling drained, like your energy is used up, or you're exhausted.

The second one is feeling more distant from your job, or negative and cynical about it.

And the third one is feeling less effective at your work.

*[on screen: burnout, as the WHO describes it / exhaustion / distance or cynicism about your job / feeling less effective at work / source: WHO, ICD-11]*

The WHO says this word is about work, and it shouldn't be used to describe other areas of life.

And the WHO doesn't classify burnout as a medical condition. It lists it as an occupational phenomenon, which means something connected to your work.

I'm not a doctor, so I can't tell you if what you're feeling is burnout.

If you heard those three signs and saw yourself in them, please talk to a doctor or someone you trust before you plan a bigger 2027.

*[optional line: And if you're okay, the next part is for you, because this is where most plans go wrong.]*

What I would tell you is to put rest in your plan as its own item, the same way you'd put a deadline.

If you're working and studying, or working two jobs, leave space in the plan.

A plan that's full from the first week of January is very hard to keep going until March.

### Step 2, map the seasons of your 2027

The second step of the reset is to map the seasons of your year before you set any goals.

Every year has busy seasons and lighter seasons, and most of us already know some of them.

For example, this is what I already know about my own 2027.

I'm doing my master's in Human-Computer Interaction at Tallinn University, and I also work full-time as a developer.

The plan is to clear all my other courses this autumn, so that from the spring of 2027, school is only my thesis.

That changes what my spring looks like, and the goals I set have to fit around it.

*[on screen: a 12-month strip / January to June marked "thesis + full-time work"]*

So take your calendar and mark what you already know about next year.

That could be exams, a busy season at work, a wedding you're travelling for, the months your kids are home, or a move.

Then, for each area you circled, set one or two goals, and put each goal where it fits.

A goal that needs a lot of time goes in a lighter season.

In a heavy season, your goal might be to keep something small going, like reading a few pages a day, and save the big new thing for later.

And make each goal something you can check.

"Read more" is hard to check at the end of the year.

"Read one book a month" is easy to check.

### Step 3, turn each goal into an if-then plan

The third step of the reset is to turn each goal into an if-then plan, and it's the step with the strongest research behind it.

This idea comes from Peter Gollwitzer, a psychology professor who has studied goals for decades.

He calls these plans implementation intentions.

The form is, "If situation Y happens, then I will do Z."

So you decide in advance when and where you'll act, instead of deciding again every day.

*[on screen: IF (when and where) ... THEN I WILL (what I'll do)]*

For example, "read more" becomes, "If I sit down to eat, then I'll read instead of watching something."

That one is how I read. When I eat, I read, instead of putting something on to watch.

Another one could be, "If it's Sunday evening, then I'll plan my week."

Or, "If I open my laptop in the morning, then I'll work on my most important task before I open email."

The situation becomes your reminder, so the decision is already made when the moment comes.

*[optional line: And this has been tested many times, by many researchers.]*

In 2006, Gollwitzer and another researcher, Paschal Sheeran, combined the results of 94 tests of if-then plans.

People who made if-then plans reached their goals more often than people who only set the goal.

The researchers described the effect as medium to large.

In plain words, it made a clear difference.

One more thing I'd do is write an if-then plan for the moment your goal usually goes wrong.

For example, "If I get home tired and reach for my phone, then I'll put it on the charger in the other room first."

### Step 4, put your plan where it can remind you

The fourth step of the reset is to put your plan where it can remind you, because a plan only helps if it shows up at the right moment.

For some people, that's the calendar on their phone.

For other people, it's an alarm, or a sticky note on the fridge.

For me, I'm building myself a little habit app.

It has a Pomodoro timer, windows when social media is blocked, my wake-up and sleep times, and streaks for my habits.

*[on screen: a quick look at the habit app, if you want to show it]*

A Pomodoro timer comes from the Pomodoro Technique, which Francesco Cirillo came up with.

You work for 25 minutes, and then you take a short break.

You don't need to build an app to do any of this.

What matters is that your if-then plans have a place where they meet you during the day.

And keep it simple enough that you'll still be using it in March.

If your phone is the thing that keeps pulling you away from your plans, I made a video on what I do instead of doomscrolling, and I'll link it.

### Step 5, a weekly review keeps the plan going

The last step of the reset is a weekly review, and I think it's the step that keeps a new year plan going after January.

A fresh start gives you a push, and that push doesn't last all year.

The weekly review comes from David Allen's book, Getting Things Done.

Once a week, you sit down and go through three things, which he calls get clear, get current and get creative.

Get clear means emptying everything out of your head, your notes and your inbox, so nothing is floating around.

Get current means updating your lists and your calendar, so they match what's true this week.

Get creative means looking ahead and thinking about what you want to do next.

*[on screen: weekly review (David Allen) / get clear / get current / get creative / + check your if-then plans]*

For your 2027 plan, I'd add one more thing to it.

Look at your if-then plans, keep the ones that worked, and change the ones that didn't.

And remember the fresh start research from Dai, Milkman and Riis.

The start of a new week was one of those fresh-start dates in their data too.

So if you do your review at the start of your week, you get a small fresh start every single week, instead of waiting a whole year for the next one.

So tell me in the comments, what's one area of your life you want to be more productive in, in 2027?

ideas.script:
### Open

I was telling someone the other day that I have achieved flow states so many times in my life, even before I knew what flow state was.

I've had times in my life where I literally got into states that I would describe as flow states, and I really enjoy being in that state.

I haven't been in that state as consistently as I would want, over the past few years at least.

Then I was watching this Arthur Brooks video about how your phone addiction is keeping you from achieving flow state, and he has a test in it that I want you to try with me.

And of course, in this video, we'll talk about what flow state even is, what your phone does to it, and how to get back into it.

### What flow state is

So what is flow state?

Flow is the state where you're so absorbed in what you're doing that everything else drops away, and when you look up, hours have passed.

The idea comes from a psychologist called Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi.

*[on screen: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (MEE-high CHEEK-sent-me-high), psychologist, author of "Flow" (1990)]*

He spent years studying the moments when people enjoyed what they were doing the most.

A lot of the people he talked to described those moments as being carried along by a current, and that's where the name flow comes from.

Csikszentmihalyi and his colleague Jeanne Nakamura described six things people experience in flow.

*[on screen: 1. intense focus on the present / 2. action and awareness merge / 3. you stop watching yourself / 4. a sense of control / 5. time feels different / 6. the activity is rewarding in itself]*

Three of them are the ones you'll recognise.

The first one is intense focus on what you're doing right now.

All your attention is in the task.

The second one is that time feels different.

Usually it flies. You sit down after lunch, and the next time you look up, it's dark outside.

The third one is that the activity feels rewarding in itself.

Csikszentmihalyi called this autotelic, which means you'd want to do it even if nobody paid you or praised you for it.

Now, flow doesn't show up just because you want it to.

In the research, it tends to happen when three conditions are in place.

*[on screen: the 3 conditions for flow / 1. a clear goal / 2. immediate feedback / 3. a challenge that matches your skill]*

The first condition is a clear goal. You know what you're trying to do right now.

The second is immediate feedback. You can tell, moment by moment, whether what you're doing is working.

The third is a challenge that matches your skill. The task is hard enough to stretch you, but not so hard that you give up.

Think about a footballer in the middle of a match.

The goal is clear, literally.

Every pass tells them straight away if it worked.

And a match against a good team stretches them without crushing them.

If a task is too easy for you, you get bored. If it's too hard, you get anxious.

Flow happens in between those two.

### Arthur Brooks's one-hour phone test

Arthur Brooks, a social scientist who studies happiness, has a simple test for whether you're addicted to your phone.

He shares it in his Big Think video, "Your phone addiction is keeping you from achieving flow state."

Put your phone away for one hour, and count how many times you think about it.

If it's more than once every five minutes, he says you're addicted.

*[on screen: Arthur Brooks's test / put your phone away for 1 hour / count how many times you think about it / more than once every 5 minutes = addicted]*

Once every five minutes is twelve times in an hour.

So if the thought "let me just check my phone" comes thirteen times in that hour, by his test, you're there.

Brooks also talks about how almost nobody believes they're addicted to their phone.

My screen time is already low compared to the average person.

But I still want it lower, because when I look at what that time gives me, I don't see the benefit.

And this test doesn't ask about your screen time at all.

It asks how often your phone takes your mind, even when it's not in your hand.

"Addicted" is Brooks's word. Phone addiction isn't an official medical diagnosis, so I'm using this test as a mirror to look at myself, and not to diagnose anybody.

So try it after this video, and tell me your number in the comments.

### How your phone competes with the three conditions of flow

Flow tends to happen when you have a clear goal, immediate feedback, and a challenge that matches your skill.

I think your phone competes with each one of those conditions.

Start with the clear goal.

When you sit down to work, you have one goal. Finish this chapter. Fix this bug. Write this section.

Your phone comes with a hundred small goals of its own.

Reply to this message. See who liked your post. Watch the video your friend just sent.

None of them is the goal you sat down with, and every one of them asks for a bit of your attention.

Then there's feedback.

Real work often gives you slow feedback. You write a paragraph, and you're not sure yet if it's any good.

Your phone gives you feedback all the time. A like, a reply, a new video that starts playing on its own.

It's quicker and it's easier, and I think that's why your real work can feel like nothing is happening when the phone is next to it.

And then there's the challenge.

Scrolling has almost no challenge, and that's part of why it feels relaxing.

This connects to something Csikszentmihalyi found that surprised me.

In a 1989 study with Judith LeFevre, they followed 78 working adults for a week, using pagers that beeped at random times and asked people what they were doing and how they felt.

Most of the flow experiences people reported happened while they were working, and very few happened in their free time.

*[on screen: "the great majority of flow experiences are reported when working, not when in leisure" (Csikszentmihalyi and LeFevre, 1989)]*

But people were more motivated in their free time than at work.

So the things that give us flow usually take effort, and the thing we want in the moment is usually the easy thing.

And the easiest thing in the room is usually the phone.

*[optional line: And your phone can pull at your attention even when you don't touch it. That's the next study.]*

### A notification can distract you even if you don't check it

A phone notification can distract you even if you never pick up the phone.

In 2015, Cary Stothart and his colleagues at Florida State University gave 166 students an attention task on a computer.

Numbers flashed on the screen, and they had to press a key for every number except 3.

While the students worked, the researchers called or texted some of the students' own phones.

Nobody answered, and nobody read anything.

The students who got a call or a text made more mistakes on the task than the students who got nothing.

*[on screen: a call or text you don't answer = more mistakes on an attention task (Stothart, Mitchum and Yehnert, 2015)]*

So just getting the notification was enough to pull their attention away.

Then in 2016, Kostadin Kushlev, Jason Proulx and Elizabeth Dunn tested this in everyday life.

221 university students spent one week with their phone alerts on and their phone close by.

They spent another week with alerts off, and the phone out of sight.

In the week with alerts on, they reported more inattention and more hyperactivity.

*[on screen: alerts on = more inattention and hyperactivity, self-reported (Kushlev, Proulx and Dunn, CHI 2016)]*

Those were the students' own reports, and the researchers were clear that this doesn't mean notifications cause ADHD.

*[optional cut starts here: brain drain lines, about 55 words. Clip 14 needs them.]*

You might also have heard of a 2017 study that said just having your phone on your desk drains your brainpower, even when it's switched off.

Later studies that tried to repeat it got mixed results, and some found no effect at all.

So I won't build anything on it. The notification studies are the ones I would lean on.

*[optional cut ends here]*

### The phone interruptions we give ourselves

A lot of phone interruptions don't come from the phone. They come from us.

Gloria Mark is a researcher at the University of California, Irvine, who studies attention and interruptions.

She has said, "These kinds of self-interruptions happen almost as frequently as people are interrupted from external sources."

*[on screen: "These kinds of self-interruptions happen almost as frequently as people are interrupted from external sources." (Gloria Mark)]*

A self-interruption is you, in the middle of a task, picking up your phone with nothing pinging at all.

She has also said that when people get a lot of interruptions from outside in an hour, they keep interrupting themselves even after the outside interruptions slow down.

So a day full of pings can teach you to keep checking, even after the pings stop.

And every check costs you something when you come back to your work.

Sophie Leroy, a researcher who studies how people work, called it attention residue.

When you move from one task to another, part of your attention stays on the first one.

So you check one message, you go back to your work, and part of your mind is still on that message.

I talk about attention residue more in my video on switching between apps, so I'll link it.

Now put that together with flow.

Flow needs a long stretch of attention on one thing.

If your mind goes to the phone every few minutes, and every check leaves a bit of residue behind, you rarely get that long stretch.

### Why we reach for the phone at the hard part

Have you noticed when you usually pick up your phone while you're working?

For a lot of us, it's at the hard part.

It's the sentence that won't come out, or the bug you can't find, or the paragraph you've read three times and still don't understand.

That moment feels uncomfortable, and the phone makes the feeling go away straight away.

Arthur Brooks talks about this in his video too.

Part of it is about how we use technology to numb uncomfortable feelings, like boredom, and he argues that those feelings have a purpose.

And for flow, I think that purpose is very clear.

Flow needs a task that stretches you, and that uncomfortable feeling is often what being stretched feels like.

So if you reach for your phone every time the work gets hard, you leave right around the point where flow could start.

*[optional cut starts here: monkey mind lines, about 30 words. Clip 19 needs them.]*

Brooks contrasts flow with what he calls the monkey mind.

Monkey mind is an old phrase for a restless mind that keeps jumping from one thing to the next.

*[optional cut ends here]*

### How to get back into flow state

So how do you get back into flow state?

These are the things I would tell you, and I'm working on them myself.

The first one is to take Arthur Brooks's one-hour test, so you know where you're starting from, and write your number down.

The second one is to turn your alerts off and put the phone out of sight.

In the Kushlev study, that was the week the students reported less inattention.

Do Not Disturb is a good start, and if you can, put the phone in another room.

The third one is to set up the three conditions for flow before you start.

Give your session one clear goal.

"Work on my project" is too big. "Write the first draft of the introduction" is clear.

Then find a way to see your progress quickly, like a word count going up, tests passing, or small steps you can tick off.

And pick a level of challenge that stretches you a little.

If the task is too easy, give yourself a time limit. If it's too hard, break off a smaller piece.

*[optional line: The next one is the one I think most of us skip.]*

The fourth one is to give flow enough time.

I don't think flow will show up in the ten minutes between two meetings, so block an hour or more if you can.

The fifth one is to stay with the hard part.

When the work gets hard and you want your phone, write the urge down on a piece of paper, and keep going for a few more minutes. See if it passes.

And the sixth one comes from Arthur Brooks.

In May 2026, he told CNN that his tech-free times are the first hour of the day, mealtimes, and the last hour before bed.

He also suggests turning off notifications, and setting your phone to grayscale, so the screen is less interesting to look at.

*[on screen: grayscale on iPhone / Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size > Color Filters > Grayscale]*

I read while I eat instead of watching something, and there is always a book in my bag.

So tell me in the comments, what was your number on the one-hour test? And when was the last time you were in flow?
