ideas.script:
### Open

I noticed one thing about Nigerian students.

When I make a video that talks about Nigerians studying abroad, there are so many people in the comment section talking about how they want to pay me for consultation.

Please, why are we so obsessed with paying people for consultation?

You don't have to pay anybody for consultation.

So in this video, I'll show you where the free information is, how to apply for a master's abroad by yourself, the email I'd send to a programme manager, and the red flags that tell you an agent is about to scam you.

### You don't need to pay for study abroad consultation

If you want to study abroad, you don't need to pay anybody for consultation.

Don't let anybody scam you.

You have the school.

The school has their website.

You can write an email to them if you are confused about anything.

A lot of these consultants are doing exactly what you can do for yourself.

They go to the same website you can go to.

They read the same requirements page, and they fill the same application form.

They're not doing anything for you that you can't do.

So just find the school, apply to the school.

In fact, you can reach out to the programme manager of the school, write an email, and you will get actual responses.

A programme manager is the person, or the small team, that runs the programme at the university. Their email is usually right there on the programme page.

I applied for my master's by myself.

I'm doing a master's in Human-Computer Interaction at Tallinn University, in Estonia.

I also got into a computer science master's, and I chose HCI.

And I don't have a computer science bachelor's. My degree is in chemistry.

Nobody applied for me.

So no, please, you don't need to pay me for consultation either.

### Where to find free, official study abroad information

If you want to apply to study abroad by yourself, you need to know where the free, official information is.

The first place is always the university's own website.

Find the page for the exact programme you want, and read everything on it. The requirements, the deadlines, the fees, and how to apply.

A lot of universities also have a page for applicants from specific countries. Tallinn University, for example, has a page just for applicants from Nigeria.

Then a lot of countries have an official website for international students.

*[on screen: Study in Estonia / Study in Germany + DAAD / Study in NL (Nuffic) / Campus France Nigeria / EducationUSA / Erasmus Mundus catalogue]*

There's Study in Estonia.

There's Study in Germany, where you can search programmes through the DAAD database or the Higher Education Compass, which lists more than 20,000 degree programmes.

There's Study in NL for the Netherlands, run by Nuffic.

For France, Campus France has offices in Nigeria, in Abuja and in Lagos.

For the US, EducationUSA has advising centres in Nigeria. The Lagos centre says it runs free counselling sessions every Wednesday.

And for Erasmus Mundus, the European Union has a catalogue of the joint master's programmes it supports.

I want to talk about three of these properly.

Study in Estonia tells you to contact the admission office at the university directly if you have questions about a programme.

It also says one online application can cover several programmes, and that application fees at Estonian universities range from 0 to 120 euros, and they're non-refundable.

So yes, you might pay a fee. You pay it to the university, through the university's own system.

The Erasmus Mundus catalogue doesn't take applications at all. It tells you to go to each programme's official website and contact the consortium, which is the group of universities that runs it.

Most of them take applications between October and January, for the next academic year. If you want scholarships, I made a full video on scholarships for African students in Europe.

And Campus France and EducationUSA are the ones you can actually walk into in Nigeria and ask questions, so you don't need a middleman to talk to them.

All of this is as of October 2026, so check the official page before you apply.

### How to apply for a master's abroad by yourself

If you want to apply for a master's abroad by yourself, this is how I would do it.

First, find the programme.

For me, I saw the programme lead of my programme posting on LinkedIn, and I decided that was the programme I wanted.

So follow the people who run the programmes you like. You'll learn a lot about the programme before you even apply.

Second, read the whole programme page, then read the page for your country, then the page about the English test.

Third, make a list of every document they ask for, with the deadline next to it.

Before I moved, I had docs and spreadsheets everywhere. That's what a consultant would do for you anyway, and you can do it in one evening.

Fourth, if something isn't clear, email the programme. I'll show you the email in a second.

Fifth, apply early.

My programme's application page says that if you apply as soon as possible, the admission specialists can give you feedback before the deadline, and you get a chance to update your application.

*[on screen: HCI at Tallinn University, autumn 2027: applications 1 Nov 2026 to 1 Mar 2027]*

That feedback is free. It comes from the people who actually decide.

### How to email a programme manager before you apply

If you're confused about anything when you're applying to study abroad, you can email the programme manager. This is the kind of email I would send.

*[on screen: the email template]*

*[on screen: code]*

```
Subject: Question about the MSc [programme name], autumn 2027 intake

Hello,

My name is [your name], and I'm planning to apply for the MSc [programme name] for the autumn 2027 intake.

I have a bachelor's degree in [your degree] from [your university] in Nigeria, and I have worked as a [your role] for [number] years.

I have read the requirements on the programme page, and I have one question. [Your question. For example: Would my work experience in software development count for the "previous experience" requirement?]

Thank you for your time.

Kind regards,
[your name]
```

Keep it short.

Say who you are in one or two lines.

Ask one or two clear questions.

And please, read the page first. If the answer is already on the page, you're asking them to read it to you.

For my programme, the email is on the programme page. It's hci-studies@tlu.ee.

Every programme has its own, so look for the contact on the page of the programme you want.

### You can write your motivation letter yourself

A lot of people pay someone to write their motivation letter for them, and I don't think you need to.

My main advice for the application is to sell your work and your experience well.

In the motivation letter, sell your experience and your passion.

If you like the programme enough, you won't find it hard to write.

Mine was so long that I had to keep cutting it.

And be original.

A consultant can't write your passion for you, because they don't know what you've done or why you want this.

The UK's Migration Advisory Committee spoke to international graduates for a 2024 review, and one of them said about their personal statement, "I think the agency wrote it for me."

I made a full video on doing a master's in tech without a CS bachelor's, where I go through the motivation letter and the interview for my programme properly.

### You already have an interview, you don't need consultation

Someone recently replied on one of my videos, and they were like, oh yeah, they already have an interview, and they want to pay me for consultation for the interview.

Like, bro, you already got to the point where you have an interview.

The reason why you have an interview with these people in the first place is because they thought you were worth interviewing.

You have impressed them to that point.

You just have to continue doing whatever it is that you did to that point.

You don't need any consultation.

For my programme, on the current admission page, the interview is 60 percent of your score, and it's mostly follow-up questions about you and what you've done.

Nobody can answer those for you.

Of course you can check and ask people.

When I was about to do my interview, I did some mock interviews with some people that were doing the programme as well.

But not in a way where I depended on them, like, oh, I need to do this for me to be selected.

So ask people. Practise out loud. Just don't hand your confidence to somebody you're paying.

### Study abroad agent scams and the red flags

Study abroad agent scams are real, and they've hurt real students.

In 2023, Canada set up a task force after hundreds of international students faced removal because their study permit applications had fake letters of acceptance.

Canada's immigration department said those cases involved unauthorised consultants who gave their clients fraudulent acceptance letters.

And this is the line from the Canadian government I want you to remember.

"The onus remains on applicants to provide truthful information on their applications even if a third party is preparing it."

So if your agent lies, you're the one who carries it.

*[optional line]*

And if you think this only happens to other countries, Nigeria's own government has warned about it.

In October 2022, Nigeria's Ministry of Foreign Affairs warned about "unscrupulous elements parading themselves as agents" selling admissions and jobs in Northern Cyprus, and said "many young Nigerians have become stranded."

Then in November 2025, the UK, Canada and Australia started a joint campaign against visa fraud, and they launched it in Nigeria.

They named the red flags.

*[on screen: red flags: excessive fees / pressure to pay quickly / promises of jobs without proper qualifications / offers to bypass standard requirements / a "guaranteed" visa]*

Demands for excessive fees.

Pressure to pay quickly.

Promises of jobs without proper qualifications.

Offers to bypass the standard requirements.

And promises of guaranteed visas. The missions said nobody can guarantee a visa.

I would add two of my own.

If someone guarantees you admission, that's a red flag, because the university decides that, and they score everybody.

And if an agent creates your application account and won't give you the login, that's a red flag. That's your application. You should be able to open it yourself.

### When paying for study abroad help is okay

Now, I'm not saying every study abroad agent is a scammer, because that's not true.

Some universities work with agents officially, and the university pays them.

Loughborough University in the UK, for example, says its agents "receive a commission-based payment from Loughborough University for every student they have supported."

The University of Bedfordshire says "agents are paid by the university on a commission basis once you enrol."

In the UK, there's a sector framework for agents called the Agent Quality Framework, and from April 2026, the Home Office's guidance says universities that use agents have to commit to its main principles.

But even the UK's Migration Advisory Committee, in its 2024 review of the Graduate route, said "agents simply do not have the same incentives as universities," and that relying on agents "may lead to individuals paying for unnecessary add-ons."

So if you decide to use someone, this is what I would do.

Ask the university directly if they work with that agent. A lot of universities list their approved agents on their website.

Ask exactly what you're paying for, and who else is paying them.

And keep your own logins, your own email, and your own documents.

If you have the time to read a page and write an email, I believe you can do this yourself.

Have you ever paid for study abroad consultation? Tell me in the comments what you paid for, and if it was worth it.

ideas.script:
### Open

You want to know how much a master's in Estonia costs, so you type it into Google.

The first result gives you a number, you take a screenshot, and you're done.

That's searching, and a lot of us stop right there.

In this video, I'll show you how to research any topic properly, using that one question all the way through.

I'm a master's student writing a thesis, and I research every video on this channel, so this is how I check things.

### Searching vs researching

The difference between searching and researching is the first thing to get right.

I learned to see it this way from Joy Ogide, a creator I really like.

Her video "How to research like a professional" was the first video of hers I ever watched, it's the reason I found her channel, and it's linked in the description.

She explains that searching is when you look something up, read the first few results, and stop.

Researching is when you also ask where the information came from, who first said it, what people agree on, what they disagree on, and what's still missing.

She breaks research into four levels.

*[on screen: Joy Ogide's four levels of research. 1. Surface 2. Context 3. Strategic 4. Original intent]*

The surface level is your first look, with Google or AI.

The context level is where you track down your sources and where the idea came from.

The strategic level is where you compare your sources and look for the common ground and the gaps.

And the original intent level is where you add something of your own, even if it's only a question.

In this video, I want to go further, into what researchers actually do at each of those levels.

### Start with a question you can answer

Proper research starts with a question that's specific enough to answer.

"How much does a master's in Estonia cost?" is too wide.

Cost for who? At which university? Only tuition, or rent and food as well? And starting in which year?

In research, this is called your research question, and when you write a thesis, it's one of the first things you have to pin down.

So I'd rewrite it like this.

*[on screen: "How much tuition would a non-EU student pay for a master's in Human-Computer Interaction at Tallinn University, starting in 2027?"]*

Now the question tells you exactly what to look for.

And it shows you what you're not answering yet.

Rent and food are a second question, and you can research that one after.

### Go to the original source

When you research anything, find out where the information started.

Sources come in three types.

Primary sources are the original. The university's own fee page, the actual study, the law itself, or the person who was there.

Secondary sources talk about the original. A news article about a study, a blog post about tuition, or a YouTube video, including this one.

Tertiary sources sum up lots of other sources, like Wikipedia or an encyclopedia.

When you need a number or a rule, try to get to the primary source.

For our question, the primary source is Tallinn University's own tuition page.

A quick way to find a page like that is to search inside one website.

On Google, you type site:, then the website's address, then your search words.

*[on screen: site:tlu.ee tuition fees]*

You can also type site:.ee to see only Estonian websites, or site:.gov.ng to see only Nigerian government websites.

When I checked Tallinn University's page in October 2026, it listed the Human-Computer Interaction master's at 7,000 euros a year for non-EU students starting in 2027.

*[on screen: Tallinn University tuition page, checked October 2026. HCI master's, non-EU students, starting 2027: €7,000 a year]*

Then check the date.

Fees and rules change, and an old blog post can stay near the top of Google for years.

For example, the University of Tartu says that from 2026/2027, it doesn't offer tuition waivers to new students from outside the EU anymore.

So a blog from a few years ago telling you about Tartu's tuition waivers would send you the wrong way.

### Check who is behind a source

Before you trust a source, find out who is behind it.

Who wrote it, and how do they know what they're saying?

The fastest way to check is to leave the page and search for the person or the organisation in a new tab.

Two researchers at Stanford, Sam Wineburg and Sarah McGrew, found that professional fact checkers do exactly this, and I go through that study in my video on how to think clearly.

The next thing to ask is whether anyone gains if you believe it.

With study abroad costs, some of the pages you'll find are written by agencies that sell application help.

It doesn't make them wrong, but check their numbers against the school's own page.

Money can sit behind science too.

In 2016, Cristin Kearns and her colleagues at UCSF published old industry documents showing that in the 1960s, a sugar industry group paid Harvard researchers to write a review on diet and heart disease.

*[on screen: the review: New England Journal of Medicine, 1967 / the documents: Kearns, Schmidt and Glantz, JAMA Internal Medicine, 2016]*

According to the UCSF team, the industry set the review's goal and saw drafts, and the review put the blame on fat and played down sugar.

And the sugar money wasn't disclosed in the paper.

So when you read a study, look for the funding section, which is usually near the end.

### Peer review, preprints and citation chasing

If your topic has research papers in it, the first thing to know is the difference between a peer-reviewed paper and a preprint.

Peer review means other experts in the field read and checked the paper before a journal or a conference published it.

A preprint is a paper the authors put online before that check, on websites like arXiv.

Preprints are useful because science moves fast, but treat them as "not checked yet".

In July 2023, a team in South Korea posted two preprints on arXiv saying they had made LK-99, a superconductor that worked at room temperature and normal pressure, and it went viral.

By August, Nature reported that an impurity called copper sulfide explained what the team had seen.

And when a lab in Germany grew pure crystals of LK-99, they were an insulator, which is the opposite of a superconductor.

*[optional line: And the second thing is the one I use the most when I'm reading for my thesis.]*

The second thing is citation chasing.

When you find one good paper, look at its reference list.

That's backward chasing. You go back to the older work it was built on.

Then look at who cited it afterwards.

On Google Scholar, there's a "Cited by" link under each result, and that's forward chasing. It shows you the newer work, including anyone who later disagreed.

*[on screen: backward = the papers it cites / forward = the papers that cite it ("Cited by" on Google Scholar)]*

I show you how I find and read papers in my video on how to read research papers.

### Compare your sources

Once you have a few good sources, compare them, and Joy Ogide calls this the strategic level.

If several independent sources say the same thing, you can trust it more.

But the word independent matters a lot.

Sometimes ten websites agree because they all copied from the same one place, and that's called circular reporting.

My favourite example is the toaster.

In 2012, some students in the UK edited Wikipedia to say that a Scottish man called Alan MacMasters invented the electric toaster in 1893.

It wasn't true.

But newspapers repeated it, books repeated it, and a primary school in Scotland even held a day in his honour.

It lasted about ten years, until 2022, when a teenager got suspicious of the photo on the Wikipedia page.

*[on screen: the Alan MacMasters toaster hoax, 2012 to 2022 (BBC News, November 2022)]*

So when your sources agree, check if each one found it themselves, or if they all point back to the same place.

And when your sources disagree, ask why before you pick a side.

With our tuition question, you might see one site saying Estonia is free, another saying 4,000 euros, and another saying 7,000.

Tallinn University's own page lists 4,000 euros a year for EU students and 7,000 for non-EU students in the HCI programme. Both numbers are correct, for different people.

Comparing sources also shows you the gaps, like the Estonian police's student guide saying you need 880 euros a month in income for a study permit, which the tuition page never mentions.

### How to use AI for research without getting fooled

AI is really good at the surface level of research, but AI tools often get their sources wrong.

In March 2025, Klaudia Jaźwińska and Aisvarya Chandrasekar at Columbia's Tow Center for Digital Journalism tested eight AI search tools.

They gave each tool a quote from a news article and asked it to name the article, the publisher, the date and the link.

Across 1,600 tries, the tools got it wrong more than 60% of the time, and they rarely said they weren't sure.

Then in October 2025, a study led by the BBC and the European Broadcasting Union checked more than 3,000 answers about the news from ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini and Perplexity.

45% of the answers had at least one significant issue, and 31% had serious problems with their sources.

*[on screen: Tow Center, March 2025: wrong in over 60% of 1,600 tests / EBU and BBC, October 2025: 45% had a significant issue, 31% had sourcing problems]*

Use AI to get the big picture, and to learn the words people use for your topic, so you can search better.

Ask it for its sources, and open every single one.

Check that the page says what the AI said it says.

And for a number or a rule, the primary source has the final word.

There are tools built for research, like Claude Science and Elicit, and I reviewed Claude Science in another video, but you still open the paper.

And AI can also make up citations completely, which I talk about in my video on how I use AI as a master's student.

### Keep notes while you research

Keeping notes while you research saves you from finding the same thing twice.

Before I moved to Estonia, I had docs and spreadsheets everywhere, and I still got surprised by a lot when I arrived.

So for every fact you find, I'd write down four things.

What it says, the link, the date you checked it, and whether it's a primary or a secondary source.

*[on screen: "HCI tuition, non-EU, from 2027: €7,000 a year / tlu.ee/en/tuition-fees / checked Oct 2026 / primary"]*

The date matters because pages change.

Next year, that fee page might say something different, and your note tells you when it was true.

For research papers, a reference manager like Zotero keeps them all in one place, and I talk about it in my video on reading research papers.

### Add your own question

The last step of researching any topic is adding your own question, and Joy Ogide calls this the original intent level.

After all your sources, ask what's still missing.

With our example, maybe you still want to know if the fee could change in your second year, so ask the people who know and email the programme manager.

The school's website and the programme managers answer these questions, and you don't need to pay anyone for that.

In academic research, that missing question is where new research starts.

A thesis is basically a question the sources haven't fully answered yet, and mine is on the cognitive cost of switching between productivity tools.

So tell me in the comments, what's one thing you believed for years and later found out wasn't true?

ideas.script:
### Open

What happens to your Instagram, your Google account and all your photos when you die?

I know, this is gonna sound weird.

But I saw a TikTok where someone found this in their Instagram settings, a setting for what happens to your account after you die.

And as someone studying human-computer interaction, I couldn't stop thinking about it.

So in this video, I'll show you what designing for death means, what goes wrong when apps forget that people die, what the big apps offer today, what the law says, and the one setting I think you should turn on today.

### What designing for death means

Designing for death starts with one question. What happens when your user dies?

One of the things that led to accessibility in design is when people started asking questions like, what if my user is blind? What if my user needs this, or needs that?

And asking those questions has established a standard for accessibility in UX, UI, and design. Things like the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines that a lot of websites follow today came out of that kind of thinking.

But one of the parts that I've started to think about is designing for death.

What happens when your users die? How do you design for the death of your user?

It turns out researchers in my field have been asking this for more than fifteen years.

In 2009, Michael Massimi and Andrea Charise wrote a short paper for CHI, which is the biggest conference in human-computer interaction.

And they gave the idea a name. Thanatosensitivity.

Thanatos is the Greek word for death.

They described it as an approach that "actively integrates the facts of mortality, dying, and death into HCI research and design."

In plain words, you design with the fact that the people using your product will die one day, and that other people will be left with everything they leave behind.

Massimi went on to work with bereaved parents, and in a 2012 interview with the University of Toronto, he said something about Facebook that I keep thinking about.

"Seeing a friend complain about a mediocre latte while you are mourning the loss of your child just doesn't work."

*[on screen: Massimi & Charise, CHI 2009 / "thanatosensitivity" / thanatos = death]*

And this isn't a small problem.

In 2019, Carl Öhman and David Watson at the Oxford Internet Institute estimated that if Facebook got no new users after 2018, the dead could outnumber the living on Facebook by 2070.

In their other scenario, where Facebook keeps growing, Nigeria alone made up more than 6% of the dead profiles by the year 2100.

So if you're building for African users, this is your problem too.

### What goes wrong when an app doesn't know a user has died

So what does it look like when an app doesn't know that one of its users has died?

The first thing is reminders.

In July 2024, Amanda Silberling, a writer at TechCrunch, wrote that Facebook reminded her, twice in one week, to wish two friends who had died a happy birthday.

The title of her article was "Facebook keeps asking me to say happy birthday to dead people."

Facebook does try to prevent this. In 2019, Sheryl Sandberg, who was Facebook's chief operating officer at the time, wrote that they use AI to keep people who have died out of things like birthday reminders, even before the account is memorialized.

But neither of Silberling's friends' accounts had been memorialized, and the reminders still came.

The second thing is ads.

In December 2018, Gillian Brockell, a video editor at the Washington Post, wrote an open letter to tech companies after her baby was stillborn.

She had searched and posted about her pregnancy, and the baby ads kept coming after her loss.

A Facebook ad executive, Rob Goldman, replied that there was a setting to block ads about painful topics like parenting, and that it "still needs improvement."

The system knew so much about her life, and it had no idea about her loss.

And if you build apps, think about every automated email you send.

If you run a bookstore app, for example, is it still sending "we miss you, come back for 20% off" to someone who has died?

### Who should get into a dead person's account?

The next problem with designing for death is access. Who should get into an account after the person dies?

Think about how we secure accounts today.

A lot of us use two-factor authentication, so a code goes to your phone every time you log in somewhere new.

Now imagine the family needs the photos in that person's cloud account.

The code goes to a phone that might be locked, or switched off, or the number might be cancelled.

So the security that protected that person can lock out the people they left behind.

The other side of this is privacy, and I think it's the strongest argument against giving families everything.

A dead person's messages are also other people's messages.

When Facebook explained in 2017 why it doesn't let families read a dead person's messages, Monika Bickert from Facebook's policy team said, "In a private conversation between two people, we assume that both people intended the messages to remain private."

*[on screen: "In a private conversation between two people, we assume that both people intended the messages to remain private." Monika Bickert, Facebook, 2017]*

And courts don't all agree.

In 2018, Germany's highest court for civil cases ruled that parents could inherit the Facebook account of their 15-year-old daughter, who died after being hit by a train.

The parents wanted to read her messages to understand what happened to her.

The court said the account could be inherited, in a similar way to letters and diaries.

So on one side, a family is locked out of photos and memories. On the other side, a person might have had conversations they never wanted anyone to read.

*[optional line: So which one is right? I don't think there's one answer for everybody, and the next part shows how the big apps chose.]*

I believe the fairest answer is to let the person decide while they're alive.

And that's what the better tools try to do.

### What Facebook, Instagram, Google and Apple offer when you die

So what do the big apps offer when a user dies? This is as of October 2026.

Let's start with Facebook.

When Facebook learns that someone has died, the account can be memorialized. The word "Remembering" shows next to the person's name, nobody can log in, and the profile is kept out of things like birthday reminders and friend suggestions.

Then in February 2015, Facebook launched the legacy contact.

A big part of the research behind it came from Jed Brubaker, an HCI researcher who's now at the University of Colorado Boulder. He worked on it with Vanessa Callison-Burch at Facebook, and they wrote about it in a 2016 paper.

A legacy contact is someone you choose while you're alive. After you die, they can pin a post on your profile, change your profile and cover photos, accept friend requests, and if you allowed it, download a copy of what you shared.

They can't log in as you, and they can't read your messages.

So the privacy question from earlier is built into the design.

Brubaker said something in 2018 that I love. "I just hope that as a result of my work, death is a little bit kinder to people."

Next is Instagram, and this is what that TikTok was about.

For years, Instagram has had memorialized accounts, with "Remembering" next to the name and nobody able to log in. Immediate family can also ask Instagram to remove the account, with documents like a death certificate.

And depending on where you live, you might also see options in your Instagram settings to choose a legacy contact, or to have your account deleted after you die.

I couldn't confirm it's in every country yet, so check your own settings.

Then Google. Google has something called Inactive Account Manager.

You choose how long Google should wait, 3, 6, 12 or 18 months without you using the account.

You can pick up to 10 people, and choose what each of them gets, like your Gmail, Drive or Photos.

When the time is up, they get a link to download it, and they have three months to save it.

And if you set nothing, since December 2023 Google can delete personal accounts that haven't been used for two years, including what's inside them.

And then Apple. Apple calls it Digital Legacy, and it came with iOS 15.2 in December 2021.

The legacy contact you add gets an access key.

After you die, they need that access key and your death certificate to ask Apple for access.

They can get your photos, messages, notes, files, device backups and more.

They can't get films, music or books you bought, or anything in your iCloud Keychain, like passwords, passkeys and payment information.

And the access lasts three years from when Apple approves it. After that, the account is deleted for good.

*[on screen: Facebook keeps messages private / Apple includes messages]*

And this is the interesting part for me as a UX person.

Facebook keeps your messages private, even from your legacy contact. Apple gives your legacy contact your messages.

Two big companies looked at the same question and made opposite choices.

### What the law says about your data after you die

So what does the law say about your data after you die? Less than you'd think.

In the EU, GDPR is the big data protection law, and it doesn't cover people who have died.

Recital 27 says, "This Regulation does not apply to the personal data of deceased persons."

It leaves each country to make its own rules.

Estonia, where I live, did. Under section 9 of Estonia's Personal Data Protection Act, a person's data stays protected for ten years after they die, or twenty years if they died as a child.

And during that time, using their data usually needs the consent of close family.

Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 is different. As far as I could find, it doesn't mention people who have died at all.

*[on screen: GDPR Recital 27 / Estonia: protected 10 years after death (20 for a child) / Nigeria NDPA 2023: nothing on the dead]*

In the US, most states have passed a version of a law called RUFADAA, the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act.

One thing it says is that if you used a company's own online tool to choose who gets access to your account, that choice generally comes before what your will says.

So in the US at least, the setting inside the app can matter more than your will.

And in a country where the law says nothing about it, the app's own policy decides most of what happens.

### If you build apps, design for when your users die

If you build apps, designing for death is something you can start on in your next sprint.

I have ranted about Uber leaving Nigeria and what happened to people's data. In that video I said everybody is always about the onboarding, and nobody asks you to design the exit of users.

But what about these situations? Death is one more exit, and it will come for every single user you have.

So these are the questions I'd ask about any app I work on.

One. How does our app find out that a user has died, and who are we going to believe?

Two. Can a user choose someone to look after their account, and what can that person do and not do?

Three. Can the family get photos and files out, without logging in as the person who died?

Four. What should stop? Birthday reminders, memories, marketing emails, ads, and "we miss you" messages.

Five. What happens to payments? Is a subscription still charging the card every month?

Six. What stays private, even from family?

And seven. What words are we using? There's a big difference between a profile that says "Remembering" and an email that says "Account of deceased user."

*[optional line: And some of this is a very small change in code.]*

If you're using Laravel, for example, it can be one line in a query.

*[on screen: code]*

```
// Skip birthday reminders for memorialized accounts
$birthdays = $user->friends()
    ->whereNull('memorialized_at')
    ->whereMonth('birthday', now()->month)
    ->whereDay('birthday', now()->day)
    ->get();
```

The hard part is deciding who is allowed to set that column, and how you check.

### Set your legacy contact today

For you as a user, the one thing I'd do today is set a legacy contact.

If you have an iPhone like me, go to Settings, tap your name, then Sign-In and Security, then Legacy Contact.

*[on screen: Settings / your name / Sign-In & Security / Legacy Contact]*

For Google, go into your Google Account settings, and under Data and privacy, look for the option to make a plan for your digital legacy. That's Inactive Account Manager.

For Facebook and Instagram, search your settings for "memorialization" or "legacy contact."

Then tell the person you picked. With Apple, they'll need the access key, so make sure they know where it is.

And if you lost someone recently and this video brought it back, I'm sorry. Take your time with any of this.

So tell me in the comments, has an app ever reminded you of someone who died? And have you set your legacy contact?

ideas.script:
### Open

You write a fetch request from your frontend to your API, you open the browser, and the console shows you this.

*[on screen: code]*

```
Access to fetch at 'https://api.bookstore.com/books' from origin
'https://bookstore.com' has been blocked by CORS policy:
No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.
```

So you copy the exact same request into an API client like Apidog, and it works. You get your books back.

*[on screen: Apidog desktop app, GET https://api.bookstore.com/books, 200 OK with the books in the response]*

In this video, I'll go through why that happens, what CORS actually is, and how to fix it properly on the server, including in Laravel.

Apidog is sponsoring this video, and it's the API client I'll use to send the requests.

### Why it works in an API client but not in the browser

*[note for you: send every request in this video from the Apidog desktop app. The web version runs inside your browser, so it needs Apidog's browser extension or Cloud Agent to get around CORS, and the Cloud Agent can't reach localhost.]*

When a request works in an API client like Apidog but fails in the browser with a CORS error, it's because the blocking is done by your browser.

The Apidog desktop app isn't a browser. Neither is curl.

They send the request, get the response, and show it to you. They don't do this check at all.

Your browser does one extra check before it lets your JavaScript see the response.

And for a simple GET request like this one, the request usually did reach your server.

Your server got it, ran the code, and sent back a response with your books.

The browser received that response, looked at the headers, didn't find the permission it was looking for, and refused to hand it to your JavaScript.

That's also why the error is so unhelpful from inside your code.

For security reasons, the browser doesn't tell your JavaScript what went wrong. In Chrome, your code just gets "Failed to fetch." The real reason is only in the console.

*[on screen: Apidog: sends the request, shows you the response. Browser: sends the request, checks the response headers, then decides if your JavaScript can read it]*

*[sponsored: Apidog]*

*[on screen: Apidog desktop app with the bookstore requests saved in one folder, then the environment switcher at the top right]*

Since Apidog is sponsoring this video, let me show you a bit more of it.

You send a request, save it, and keep all your bookstore requests together in one folder, so you're not typing them again every time.

You can also set up environments. So the same requests go to localhost while you're building, and to your live API later, and you only switch the environment.

And you can keep your API docs and your tests in the same place.

If you want to try it, the link is in the description.

*[end of sponsored part]*

So what is the browser checking for? It's checking whether your page and your API are on the same origin.

### What an origin is

To understand CORS errors, you need to know what an origin is.

An origin is three things together. The scheme, the host and the port.

Take https://bookstore.com.

The scheme is https. The host is bookstore.com. And the port is 443, which is the default for https, so you don't see it written.

If any one of those three is different, it's a different origin.

*[on screen: code]*

```
https://bookstore.com/books     same origin (only the path is different)
https://api.bookstore.com       different origin (different host)
http://bookstore.com            different origin (different scheme)
https://bookstore.com:8080      different origin (different port)
```

The path doesn't count. /books and /authors on the same site are the same origin.

In our bookstore app, the frontend is on bookstore.com, and the API is on api.bookstore.com.

They both belong to us. But to the browser, they are two different origins, because the host is different.

And you see this even more when you're working locally.

Your frontend runs on localhost port 5173, and your Laravel API runs on localhost port 8000.

Same machine, same localhost, but different ports, so they are different origins.

That's why so many people meet their first CORS error on day one of a new project.

### The same-origin policy and why browsers have it

Browsers have a rule called the same-origin policy.

It says that JavaScript running on one origin generally can't read responses from a different origin.

Think about what could happen without it.

Say you're logged in to your email in one tab. Then you open some random website in another tab.

If there were no same-origin policy, that website's JavaScript could send a request to your email provider.

If your browser attached your login cookies to that request, the response would be your inbox.

And the random website could read it and send it off to its own server.

There's a second example that has nothing to do with cookies.

Your browser can reach places that a stranger on the internet can't, like your home router's settings page, or your company's internal tools that only work inside the office network.

Without the same-origin policy, any website you visit could use your browser to read those pages too.

So the same-origin policy stops a page from reading what comes back from another origin.

Sending is treated differently. A page can still send some cross-origin requests, like submitting a form to another site. What it generally can't do is read the response.

That's why, with a simple request, your request reaches the server and only the reading gets blocked.

Browsers today also have extra protections for cookies, like SameSite cookies. But the same-origin policy is the older rule, and it's the one behind your CORS error.

### What CORS is

So if the browser blocks cross-origin reads by default, how does our bookstore frontend ever get data from our own API?

That's what CORS is for. CORS stands for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing.

It's a way for a server to tell the browser which other origins are allowed to read its responses.

So CORS relaxes the same-origin policy, for the origins the server chooses.

And it works with headers.

When your frontend makes a cross-origin request, the browser adds an Origin header to say where the request is coming from.

*[on screen: code]*

```
GET /books HTTP/1.1
Host: api.bookstore.com
Origin: https://bookstore.com
```

If the server is happy for that origin to read the response, it sends back this header.

*[on screen: code]*

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://bookstore.com
Content-Type: application/json
```

The browser compares the two.

If the origin in that header matches your page's origin, or the header is a star, which means any origin, your JavaScript gets the response.

If the header is missing, or it names a different origin, you get the error. "No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource."

So when you see that message, the browser is telling you the server didn't give permission. The fix lives on the server.

### Simple requests vs preflight requests

For CORS, the browser puts cross-origin requests into two groups. Simple requests, and requests that need a preflight.

A simple request goes straight to the server. The browser sends it, then checks the response headers when they come back.

A request is simple when it uses GET, HEAD or POST, it only sets a few basic headers, and if it has a Content-Type, it's one of three. Form data, multipart form data for file uploads, or plain text.

Anything outside that needs a preflight.

So a PUT, a PATCH or a DELETE needs one. Sending an Authorization header with a token needs one. And sending JSON with a Content-Type of application/json needs one too.

That last one surprises a lot of people, because most of our API calls send JSON. So a lot of the API calls a modern frontend makes get a preflight.

And the preflight is where a lot of the confusing CORS bugs come from, so stay with me here.

A preflight is a small request the browser sends first, before your real request, to ask the server for permission. It uses the OPTIONS method.

Say our bookstore frontend wants to update a book's price.

*[on screen: code]*

```
fetch("https://api.bookstore.com/books/42", {
  method: "PUT",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "Authorization": "Bearer abc123",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ price: 15 }),
});
```

Before it sends this, the browser sends this.

*[on screen: code]*

```
OPTIONS /books/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.bookstore.com
Origin: https://bookstore.com
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization, content-type
```

It's basically asking the server, can bookstore.com send you a PUT, with these two headers?

And the server answers.

*[on screen: code]*

```
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://bookstore.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Authorization, Content-Type
Access-Control-Max-Age: 7200
```

The answer has to be a success, so a status in the 200s, and the headers have to cover what the browser asked for.

Only then does the browser send the real PUT.

If the preflight fails, your real request never leaves the browser.

So when you open the Network tab and see two requests for one fetch, an OPTIONS and then your real one, that's the preflight. Nothing is wrong.

### The main CORS headers

There are six CORS headers a server can send back.

Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, Access-Control-Max-Age and Access-Control-Expose-Headers.

*[on screen: the six headers as a list, with Allow-Origin, Allow-Methods / Allow-Headers and Max-Age highlighted]*

Access-Control-Allow-Origin says which origin can read the response.

It takes one origin, or a star. You can't put a list of origins in it.

So if your API should allow both bookstore.com and admin.bookstore.com, the server looks at the Origin of each request. If that origin is on its list, it sends that one origin back.

Most CORS libraries do this for you. They also add a header called Vary: Origin, so that a cache doesn't hand a response meant for one origin to a request from another.

Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers are the answers to the preflight.

They say which methods, like PUT and DELETE, and which request headers, like Authorization or Content-Type, the server will accept from another origin.

One small thing here. If you allow headers with a star, the Authorization header still has to be listed by name.

Access-Control-Max-Age says how long, in seconds, the browser can remember the preflight answer, so it doesn't ask again before every single request.

If you don't send it, the browser only remembers for five seconds.

And browsers put a cap on it. Chrome and other Chromium browsers cap it at two hours. Firefox caps it at twenty-four hours.

Access-Control-Expose-Headers lets your JavaScript read extra response headers, like a total count header for pagination. By default, it can only read a few basic ones.

And Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is for cookies, and it comes with a stricter rule.

### Credentials, cookies and why the star doesn't work

By default, when your frontend calls an API on another origin, fetch doesn't send your cookies.

If your bookstore uses cookie-based login, like Laravel Sanctum does for single-page apps, you have to ask for cookies on purpose.

*[on screen: code]*

```
// fetch
fetch("https://api.bookstore.com/orders", { credentials: "include" });

// or axios
axios.defaults.withCredentials = true;
```

Once a request carries credentials, the browser gets stricter.

The server has to send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

And Access-Control-Allow-Origin has to name the exact origin. A star is not allowed.

*[on screen: code]*

```
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://bookstore.com
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
```

If the server sends a star on a request that has cookies, the browser blocks the response.

The reason makes sense when you think about what the star means. The star means any website at all.

If any website could send a request with your logged-in users' cookies and read the answer, any website could read your users' private data. Their orders, their address, their account.

The same goes for methods and headers. With credentials, a star in Allow-Methods or Allow-Headers is treated as a plain star character, so you have to list them.

So if your API uses cookies, name your frontend's origin, and turn credentials on.

### What CORS can't do for your API

A lot of people set up CORS on their API and think it's now protected.

CORS is a set of rules that browsers follow. It only changes what a web page, running in a browser, is allowed to read.

An API client like Apidog doesn't follow those rules. Neither does curl, or a Python script, or another server.

So anyone can still call your API directly, with any Origin header they like, and your server will answer.

*[on screen: in Apidog, send GET https://api.bookstore.com/books with the header Origin: https://some-other-site.com, and the books still come back]*

Setting your allowed origins to only bookstore.com won't stop someone from calling api.bookstore.com from their terminal.

What protects your API is on the server. Authentication, checking that the user is allowed to do what they're asking for, and rate limiting.

CORS protects your users from other websites, inside their own browser.

I have a video on API authentication if you want to go deeper on that part.

### Common CORS mistakes and how to fix them

There are a few CORS mistakes that come up over and over, so let's go through them.

The first one is trying to fix CORS from the frontend.

Chrome's error message even suggests it. It says, if an opaque response serves your needs, set the request's mode to 'no-cors'.

*[on screen: code]*

```
fetch("https://api.bookstore.com/books", { mode: "no-cors" });
// no error, but the response is opaque
// you can't read the status or the body
```

That makes the error go away, but you get back an opaque response. Your JavaScript can't read the status or the body, so for an API call, it's useless.

Another one is adding Access-Control-Allow-Origin to your request. That's a header the server sends, so putting it on your request does nothing for CORS. And because the browser doesn't count it as a basic header, it can even trigger a preflight.

And browser extensions that turn CORS off only change your own browser. Your users won't have that extension.

The fix goes on the server, because the server is the one giving permission.

*[optional line]*

If you've been stuck on a CORS error for hours, there's a good chance it's one of the next ones.

The second mistake is using the star with cookies. If your requests send credentials, name the origin.

The third one is sneaky. Your CORS setup works, until something fails.

Say a user uploads a book cover that's too big. Your web server, like nginx, rejects it with a 413 before the request even reaches your app. Or your app is down, and the server sends back a 502 error page.

Those error responses often don't have the CORS headers, because your CORS code never ran.

So the browser shows you a CORS error, and the real problem, the 413 or the 502, is hidden behind it.

When a CORS error only happens sometimes, check the Network tab for the real status code, and check your server logs.

The fourth one is the preflight itself not being handled.

If your server sends back a 404 or a 401 for the OPTIONS request, maybe because there's no route for it, or your auth middleware runs first and rejects it, the preflight fails.

Preflight requests never carry your cookies or your token, so your server has to answer them before any login check.

And the last one is a tool a lot of people use without knowing why it works, which is a dev proxy.

If you use Vite, you can tell its dev server to forward your API calls to your backend.

*[on screen: code]*

```
// vite.config.js
export default {
  server: {
    proxy: {
      "/api": "http://localhost:8000",
    },
  },
};
```

Now your frontend calls /api/books on localhost:5173, which is its own origin.

Vite forwards that request to localhost:8000 from the server side, where there's no browser and no CORS check.

This only works in development. In production, you either set up CORS properly on your API, or you serve your API from the same origin, like bookstore.com/api.

### How to set up CORS in Laravel

If you're using Laravel, for example, CORS support is already built in.

Laravel has a middleware called HandleCors in its global middleware stack. It runs on every request, and it answers the preflight OPTIONS requests for you.

On Laravel 11 and newer, the CORS config file isn't there by default. You publish it with this command.

*[on screen: code]*

```
php artisan config:publish cors
```

On older versions, config/cors.php is already in your config folder.

This is what it looks like for our bookstore.

*[on screen: code]*

```
// config/cors.php
return [
    'paths' => ['api/*', 'sanctum/csrf-cookie'],

    'allowed_methods' => ['*'],

    'allowed_origins' => [
        'https://bookstore.com',
        'http://localhost:5173',
    ],

    'allowed_origins_patterns' => [],

    'allowed_headers' => ['*'],

    'exposed_headers' => [],

    'max_age' => 7200,

    'supports_credentials' => true,
];
```

paths is which routes get the CORS headers. By default, it's your api routes and Sanctum's CSRF cookie route. If a route isn't covered here, Laravel won't add the headers to it.

allowed_origins is the list of frontends allowed to read your responses. The default is a star. For our bookstore, I've put the live site and the local Vite dev server. In a real app, you'd usually read these from your .env file.

max_age is how long the browser can remember the preflight answer. The default is zero, so I've set it to two hours, which is the most Chrome will use anyway.

supports_credentials turns on Access-Control-Allow-Credentials. You turn it on if you use cookies, like with Sanctum's single-page app login.

And when it's on, make sure allowed_origins lists your real origins.

If you leave allowed_origins as a star with credentials turned on, Laravel sends back whatever origin asks. That means any website could read your logged-in users' responses.

And if you change this file and nothing happens, your config might be cached. Run php artisan config:clear, or run config:cache again in production.

### How to debug a CORS error

When you see a CORS error, this is the order I'd check things in.

First, open the Network tab and find the request. If there's an OPTIONS request before it, check that one first, because if the preflight fails, your real request never went out.

Look at the status code. If it's a 404, a 401, a 413 or a 500, you have a server problem showing up as a CORS error.

Then look at the response headers. Is Access-Control-Allow-Origin there, and does it match your page's origin exactly, with the same scheme and the same port?

If you're sending cookies, is Access-Control-Allow-Credentials set to true, and does the origin header name your site?

If you're sending a custom header, or using PUT or DELETE, are those in Allow-Headers and Allow-Methods?

All of these fixes go on the server.

Tell me in the comments the strangest CORS error you've ever hit, and what it turned out to be.

ideas.script:
### Why finding research papers is the hard part

If you're writing a thesis or a project, finding the right research papers can be harder than reading them.

You search your topic on Google, and you get blog posts and adverts.

Or you finally find the perfect paper, and it asks you to pay before you can read it.

So in this video, I'll show you where to search, how one good paper leads you to the rest, how to get the PDF for free and legally, and how to tell if a paper is worth your time.

We'll start with Google Scholar.

### How to search Google Scholar

Google Scholar is a free search engine for academic work, like articles, theses and books.

I think it's the best place to start, because it searches across a lot of publishers at once.

First, put a phrase in quotation marks.

If you're researching how people switch between apps, for example, search for "task switching" in quotes.

Then Google Scholar looks for those two words together, in that order.

*[on screen: a Google Scholar search for "task switching", with the quotation marks highlighted]*

Second, on the results page, you can choose to only see papers since a certain year.

If you're writing a thesis, recent papers matter, because they show you where the research is right now.

Third, once you have a search that gives you good results, set an alert.

Click the envelope icon, type your email, and click "Create alert".

Then Google Scholar emails you when new papers match that search, so you don't have to keep searching every week.

*[on screen: the envelope icon and the "Create alert" button]*

### Following citations backward and forward

When you find one good research paper, you can use it to find many more, and this is called following the citations.

I like to think of it like a family tree.

Going backward means reading the paper's reference list.

Those are the older papers it was built on, like its parents and grandparents.

Going forward means looking at the newer papers that cited it, like its children.

On Google Scholar, under each result, there's a link that says "Cited by", with a number.

*[on screen: a Google Scholar result with "Cited by", "Related articles" and "All versions" circled]*

If it says "Cited by 300", it means 300 works that Google Scholar knows about have cited that paper, and you can click it to see all of them.

Some of those newer papers will build on it, and some will disagree with it, and you want to know both.

Next to it is "Related articles", which shows you similar papers.

And you can set an alert on a "Cited by" page too, so Google Scholar emails you whenever someone new cites that paper.

### Keshav's tip for starting a literature review

If you're starting a literature review from zero, there's a tip I like from S. Keshav.

He's a computer scientist, and in 2007, while he was at the University of Waterloo, he wrote a short paper called "How to Read a Paper".

*[on screen: S. Keshav, "How to Read a Paper", ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review, 2007]*

First, he says to use a search engine like Google Scholar to "find three to five recent papers in the area."

Do a quick first read of each one, which I show you how to do in my video on how to read a research paper.

Then read their related work sections.

The related work section is the part of a paper where the authors talk about the research that came before theirs.

So someone has already done a small search for you.

If you're lucky, one of those papers points you to a survey paper, which is a paper that reviews the research on a whole topic.

Keshav writes, "If you can find such a survey, you are done."

*[optional line: "And if you don't find one, the next step is the one I find most useful."]*

If you don't find a survey, look at the reference lists of those papers.

Look for the papers and the names that keep showing up again and again.

Keshav says, "These are the key papers and researchers in that area."

Then see where those researchers publish, because, in Keshav's words, "the best researchers usually publish in the top conferences."

### arXiv and preprints

If you're in computer science or AI, a lot of the papers people share online come from arXiv.

arXiv is a free, open access site where researchers post their papers, often before a journal or a conference publishes them.

The papers on arXiv are called preprints.

Peer review is when other experts in the field read a paper and check it before it gets published.

arXiv does check papers before they go up, but arXiv itself says, "the arXiv moderation process is not a peer-review process."

So a preprint can be very good, but you can't assume it has been peer reviewed.

Read it with a bit more care.

A lot of arXiv papers get published later, so search the title on Google Scholar and click "All versions".

If there's a published version, I would read and cite that one.

### Research databases for your field

Most fields also have their own research database, and it's worth knowing the one for yours.

If you're in HCI or computer science, for example, it's the ACM Digital Library.

ACM publishes the proceedings of CHI, which ACM calls its flagship conference for human-computer interaction.

The proceedings are all the papers from a conference, collected together.

And as of the first of January 2026, ACM says all of its publications in the Digital Library are open access, so you can read them for free.

*[on screen: ACM Digital Library, all ACM publications open access since 1 January 2026]*

If you're in medicine or biology, there's PubMed, which is free to search, and it often links you to the full paper.

If you're in engineering, there's IEEE Xplore.

Anyone can search it, but a lot of the full papers need a subscription.

And Semantic Scholar is a free search tool for scientific papers, from the Allen Institute for AI.

If you ever ask an AI chatbot to find papers for you, open every single one, because a 2023 study by William Walters and Esther Wilder found ChatGPT making up references that don't exist.

### How to get a research paper for free and legally

When you find a research paper and it's behind a paywall, there are a few free and legal things to try before you pay.

The first is your university library.

Universities pay for journal subscriptions so their students and staff can read these papers.

So log in through your library website.

You can also add your university library in Google Scholar's settings, and then you'll see a link to get the paper through your library next to the results.

The second is "All versions" on Google Scholar.

Sometimes one of those versions is a free PDF, like a copy on the author's university website.

The third is the author's own website.

A lot of researchers put copies of their papers there.

The fourth is a free browser extension called Unpaywall.

When you open a paper's page, it checks whether a free, legal copy exists somewhere, and if it does, it gives you a link to it.

*[on screen: Unpaywall, unpaywall.org]*

And if none of that works, email the author.

Tell them who you are and what you're working on, and ask if they can share a copy.

I think most researchers are happy that someone wants to read their work, and the worst that can happen is that they don't reply.

### How to tell if a research paper is a good source

Before you build your work on a research paper, check if it's a good source.

The first thing I check is where it was published.

Is it a journal or a conference that people in your field know and respect?

For HCI, for example, CHI is one of those.

The second thing is whether it was peer reviewed.

A preprint can still be useful, but I'd say clearly that it's a preprint when you cite it.

The third thing is how many times it's been cited.

A lot of citations usually means people in the field know the paper.

But a paper from last year won't have many citations yet, because people haven't had time to cite it.

A paper can also be cited a lot because people disagree with it.

And citation numbers are very different from field to field.

The Leiden Manifesto, published in Nature in 2015, says to "account for variation by field in publication and citation practices."

So use citations as one clue, and read the paper to decide if it's good.

What are you researching right now? Tell me your topic in the comments, and which of these you're going to try first.

ideas.script:
### Open

These are the things I wish I knew before studying abroad, and most of them are not about your school.

*[on screen: black card "9 THINGS"]*

I moved to Tallinn, which is the capital of Estonia, in autumn 2025 for my master's degree, and I'm now in my second year.

I'll go through nine of them. One of them is how I renewed my Nigerian passport through the embassy in Sweden, and I didn't have to go to Sweden. And I'll tell you how long Estonia lets you stay after your studies end.

These are practical things based on my experience.

Emphasis on based on my experience.

I'll be using Estonia a lot as my example, but I think most of this applies regardless of the country you're going to, or at least it's good to know.

### Understand how the country runs

*[on screen: 01 / how the country runs]*

The first thing I'd tell anyone about to study abroad is to try to understand how the country they're going to runs.

So don't just be focused on your school, your programme.

Understand how things get done in the country.

In Estonia, for example, when you get here as an international student, you'll probably come on a visa.

One of the things you have to do is apply for a residence permit card.

Estonians have an ID card that everyone has, and as an international student, the residence permit card kind of works the same way.

So basically, you use it to prove who you are online, and to sign documents digitally.

You can set it up on your phone.

Banks use it, and a lot of websites here in Estonia even ask for it before you set up an account and all of that.

*[on screen: residence permit card = prove who you are online + sign documents digitally + banks and websites]*

Now, this might be different in the country you're going to, if it's not Estonia.

It might not be something as digital as that.

Things might be more manual.

So you want to know what's up.

If I come on a student visa, do I have to get the residence permit?

Or do I keep studying on my visa?

Just try to find out how it all works.

In Estonia, before your residence permit card comes, I don't even think you can start a proper job.

In Tallinn, public transport is free, but only if you're a registered Tallinn resident.

So if you're not a resident, you pay for transport.

So it influences the decisions you make in that way, and you need to understand how it works.

You also want to register your address and stuff like that.

Even if you're living in the school dormitory, you should still register that address, because you're a tenant regardless.

*[on screen: Estonia: register your address within 1 month of your permit · Tallinn: free public transport for registered Tallinn residents (as of November 2026)]*

But again, the rules can change, and every country is different.

So try to understand how the country you're going to runs, or how the city runs, and try to set things up for yourself.

Okay.

### Can you work while studying abroad?

*[on screen: 02 / work]*

Another thing to find out before you study abroad is the work situation in the country or the city you want to study in.

If you're interested in working as an international student, you need to do your research on how things work in the country you're studying in.

For example, if you're coming to Estonia to study, you can work.

According to the Police and Border Guard Board, students on residence permits for study don't need a separate work permit to work.

*[on screen: the Police and Border Guard Board line "no need for separate work permit", highlighted]*

But there are conditions attached to you working.

Even if you're working, the condition is that you have to keep studying full-time, and your work cannot get in the way of your studies.

So if you interrupt your studies, or you don't complete your programme to the required extent, then your residence permit ends 30 days after that.

*[on screen: Estonia, study residence permit: no separate work permit · keep studying full-time · studies come first]*

Also, this is another thing.

What happens after you graduate?

So if you hope to move away from the city, or maybe you hope to spend more time in the city, try to find out what the gist is.

After I graduate, how can I stay back in the country?

Do I get a work permit, and all of that?

So you have to start planning for that, or at least in a way, from the onset.

In Estonia, for example, after a residence permit for study ends, you can stay 270 more days, which is about nine months, in the country.

You can work during that time, and if you find a job, you can apply for a residence permit for work, right?

*[on screen: after your study permit ends: 270 more days (about 9 months) · doesn't apply if the permit was revoked or ended early]*

So just try to understand how it works.

### Health insurance as an international student

*[on screen: 03 / health insurance]*

Another thing you need to get right before you study abroad is health insurance as a student.

Health insurance is very important.

You don't want to be in a country or a city where you don't know so many people, where you're still trying to build a community around yourself, and you don't have health insurance.

You need that insurance.

At least from my experience, when I was coming from Nigeria, I had to buy an insurance.

It wasn't really one of those ones that cover a lot.

So yeah.

You can also try to understand how health insurance works in the country.

Is it free?

Is it subsidised for students?

In Estonia, for example, if you're a student from outside the EU, you need private health insurance.

Again, I had to buy one before I even went to apply for my visa.

If you get a job here with an employment contract, then things can change a little bit.

The employer pays social tax, and then you get state health insurance through the Estonian Health Insurance Fund, right?

*[on screen: student from outside the EU = private health insurance · employment contract = state health insurance (Tervisekassa), starting 14 days after you start work]*

But if you don't have a job that covers you, you have to get private health insurance.

So you need to put that in place, and read and understand what your private health insurance covers before you buy it.

### The weather (how dark the winter gets)

*[on screen: 04 / the weather]*

The weather.

Another thing you need to know before you study abroad is the weather.

In Estonia, for example, it can get really cold.

Winter is long.

Winter is dark.

Winter is so cold.

In Tallinn in December, you get about six hours of daylight.

*[say twice]*

*[on screen: Tallinn, December: about 6 hours of daylight]*

So try to understand how the weather works and prepare for it.

Like, really prepare for it.

I know someone here who was telling me about when they had just arrived.

In their first winter, they literally landed in the hospital.

So you want to prepare for the weather if you're coming from somewhere that is way different.

If you're coming from somewhere like Nigeria all the way to the Baltics here, it's like going from one end of the world to the other end of the world in terms of the weather.

### Finding a place to live

*[on screen: 05 / a place to live]*

Okay, that's four. The passport one is number eight, I'm getting there.

Another thing to think about before you study abroad is a place to live, and finding a place to live.

I think this is usually easy if you come as a student and your school has a dormitory, right?

I stayed in the dormitory for about a month plus, and it was really nice.

My flatmates were really nice.

But I moved out of the dormitory afterwards.

When you stay in the dormitory, of course you pay less.

Mine was about €250 a month.

But if you're someone who would like to live outside the dormitory, then you might want to roughly double that budget, right?

*[on screen: my dorm: about €250 a month · living outside it: roughly double (my experience, prices change)]*

So basically, think about what kind of living fits you, and your budget, even before you come.

It will make life easier for you.

### Learning the language

*[on screen: 06 / the language]*

If you're studying in a country where the official language is not English, you might want to consider learning the language.

Of course, you're probably studying in a programme where the language of the course is English.

But if the language of the country is not English, I think learning it helps a lot.

I was reading one of Khaled Hosseini's books, *And the Mountains Echoed*, and one of the statements that really stood out to me was this.

"If culture was a house, then language was the key to the front door, to all the rooms inside."

*[on screen: the quote + "Khaled Hosseini, And the Mountains Echoed" (hold the book up if you have it)]*

So if you really want to interact with the culture, you need to try to learn the language.

In my school this is easy, because we compulsorily have to do an Estonian A1 class.

It might not be the same in another country.

But even if it's not something that is required, I think it's always nice to interact with the culture where you're schooling through the language as well.

If you choose to spend a year, two years of your life in a place, you might as well just enjoy it.

And part of enjoying it is interacting with the culture, interacting with the language.

### Your driving licence abroad

*[on screen: 07 / your driving licence]*

Another thing to check before studying abroad is your driver's licence.

If you drive in Nigeria, you want to check if your Nigerian driver's licence can work in the country you're going to.

In Estonia, the Nigerian driver's licence is valid for 12 months from when your residency starts, and then you have to exchange it for an Estonian one.

I have exchanged mine.

Right.

*[on screen: Estonia: Nigerian licence valid 12 months from your residency start · then exchange it (generally no exams) · the old licence is handed over]*

So if driving is something you do, and you want to continue doing it while schooling, you need to understand, like, oh, what's the way to get a driver's licence in this place, and all of that.

### Renewing your Nigerian documents abroad

*[on screen: 08 / your passport from abroad]*

Another practical thing is renewing your Nigerian documents while you're not in Nigeria.

This could be any Nigerian document.

For example, your Nigerian passport.

My Nigerian passport expired some months ago, and I had to renew it.

Obviously, I wasn't going to go to Nigeria for that.

If you're an international student in another country, and you know you won't be going home frequently, then you need to do a bit of research on how to go about renewing your documents whenever they expire.

There's no Nigerian embassy in Estonia here, so I had to renew mine through the Nigerian Embassy in Stockholm, in Sweden.

And the Nigerian government has launched a contactless passport renewal option for eligible Nigerians in Europe, which is the option that I used.

So I did it in Sweden, and I didn't have to go to Sweden to do it.

### Enjoy it

*[on screen: card linking to the passport renewal video (kit 02) + the Ministry of Interior page as a receipt]*

*[on screen: 09 / enjoy it]*

Also, last but not the least, if you're schooling abroad, you also want to try to enjoy living there.

Be open-minded to enjoying things there.

There are things you would not like, and there are things you will like.

But be more open-minded to just enjoying the things that you like.

Even though you're going to be there for a short time, even if it's just for the duration of your study, and you're going to go back, you want to just enjoy the place as well.

Go for Erasmus programmes.

I've been on two Erasmus programmes so far.

Join different programmes in school, you know, meet people, enjoy it.

It's a new country, a new city.

I know that studying abroad, it will literally take your whole life if you give it, especially if you're working.

But just try to breathe the air of the country a little bit.

Okay.

*[outro: record both, we use the one that fits]*

A: And if you're Nigerian and your passport is going to expire while you're abroad, I made a whole video on how I renewed mine from Estonia, step by step. It's right here.

B: And if you're from Nigeria and you're thinking about studying in Europe, watch the video I made on what nobody warned me about studying in Europe as a Nigerian. It's right here.
