ideas.title: Why Do AI Data Centers Need So Much Water?
ideas.format: talking head with real props in hand (glass of water, phone, kettle and its scale) + receipt cards for every number + two motion graphics beside her (50,000 kettles, cooling tower)
ideas.hook: Why do AI data centers even need water?

record.where: the kitchen, at the counter, kettle in shot; window light from the side
record.how: standing, chest-up, 4K landscape, headroom and centred for a 9:16 crop; glass of water up to the lens on the first word
record.props: a clear glass of water, her phone, the kettle (plus a 3 s torch-lit close-up of the white scale inside)

ideas.script:
### Open

*[on screen: hold up a glass of water on the first word; top title box; glass clink]*

Why do AI data centers even need water?

One of the growing complaints I see on social media is how AI data centers are consuming water that should be for human usage.

*[on screen: 2-3 real headline cards, with source credit]*

And I, myself, I'm always thinking, why do they even need that much water in the first place?

And if it's only for cooling, why can't they just use seawater? I had to look that up too.

And does the water come back after they use it?

So I looked into it a little bit.

### Why AI chips get so hot

To understand why AI data centers need water, you have to start with heat.

Now, all these chips, AI chips, which include GPUs, they are made up of billions of tiny switches.

And when electricity flows through them, it turns into heat.

*[on screen: a chip, zoomed in, with "billions of tiny switches"]*

It's kind of a similar reason to why your phone gets a little bit warm when you're playing a game for too long.

*[prop: hold up your phone]*

With computers, nearly all the electricity that goes in ends up as heat.

### How much heat an AI data center makes

Now, if you scale that up to an AI data center, a big AI data center can use, say, 100 megawatts of power.

A typical electric kettle uses about 2,000 watts.

*[prop: the kettle beside you]*

So 100 megawatts is almost like 50,000 kettles boiling at the same time, all day, all night, inside the same building.

*[on screen: (motion insert): 100,000,000 W ÷ 2,000 W = 50,000 kettles, the kettles filling the screen]*

If the heat stays in the building, the chips would slow themselves down to survive, and eventually they will fail and stop working.

So the heat has to leave the building somehow, and that's where water comes in.

### Why water is so good at carrying heat

Now, data centers use water to cool down because water is very good at carrying heat.

One litre of water can soak up about 3,500 times more heat than a litre of air, for the same rise in temperature.

*[on screen: 1 litre of water ≈ 3,500 litres of air (same temperature rise)]*

And when water evaporates, it also carries away even more heat.

It's comparable to how sweating cools our body down.

Sweat evaporates off the skin, and it takes the heat away with it.

### How a data center cooling tower works

So a lot of AI data centers cool themselves the same way that our body does, using cooling towers.

Warm water from the building gets sprayed down inside the tower, while fans pull outside air through it.

Some of that water evaporates, and that cools down the rest, you know, which goes back inside to pick up more heat.

*[on screen: (motion insert): simple cooling tower diagram, warm water down, air through, vapour out the top, cool water back to the building]*

I was trying to check the scale of how much water this uses.

According to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute, a large data center can use up to 5 million gallons of water a day.

That's roughly the daily water use of a small town of about 10,000 to 50,000 people.

*[on screen: receipt card of the EESI page, the sentence highlighted: "up to 5 million gallons per day ... a town populated by 10,000 to 50,000 people"]*

So that's how much water, roughly.

*[optional part (ours, not your words; record only if you say yes in my questions)]*
> And I also wanted to know how much of that is one prompt.
> Google published a paper in August 2025 saying the median Gemini text prompt uses about 0.26 millilitres of water, which is about five drops.
> And Sam Altman wrote that an average ChatGPT query uses about one fifteenth of a teaspoon, but he didn't say how he worked it out.
> Critics say those numbers only count the water used on site for cooling, not the water used to make the electricity.
> So one prompt is small. It's the scale that people are worried about.

### Why can't data centers use seawater?

Now, from a layman's perspective, if the water is only meant for cooling, I'm thinking, why can't data centers just use any other kind of water, like seawater?

Well, most of them can't.

*[on screen: the inside of a kettle with white scale, phone torch on it]*

If you check your kettle at home, the white crust at the bottom is the minerals that were in your tap water, right?

Now, a cooling tower is evaporating water all day, so the minerals can build up.

If seawater evaporates, it just leaves salt everywhere, and salt can eat away at metal.

That's kind of why cooling towers need clean, fresh water.

### Where data center water comes from, and where it goes

*[optional line, see question 2: Google's Hamina data centre]*

Right.

The major crux of the discussion I've been seeing about AI data centers and water, mostly on social media at least, is that a lot of this data center water comes from the same public water systems that supply people's homes.

And you can make the argument that if the water is used, it evaporates, and again, it comes down as rain.

*[on screen: vapour leaves the tower, rain falls far away]*

But it doesn't go back to the same river or the same underground water that the people around it are using.

So I was just trying to understand the whole water and AI data center conversation, and that's just my understanding as of right now.

*[optional: closing comment question, then Outro A or B, see 0e]*

*[outro: record both, we use the one that fits]*

A: If you've been wondering how I actually use AI as a master's student, I made a whole video on it, and it's right here.

B: I make videos explaining tech I'm curious about, so if this was useful, the next one is right here.

ideas.title: You Want to Do Everything, So You Do Nothing
ideas.format: Talking head at the kitchen or dining table with a notepad (the loop and Ben Carson's 2x2 grid drawn live, held to the lens) + black First / Second / Third phrase cards (#29) + the book on camera (#27) + thinker cards (#26)
ideas.hook: You literally want to do everything, so you end up doing nothing.

record.where: The kitchen or dining table in the new flat (not the desk), with a calm plain wall or curtained window behind
record.how: Sitting at the table, camera across it, centred, 4K landscape from just above her head to the table, notepad and hands in the middle third for the 9:16 crop; warm and a little playful; pause between the four questions
record.props: An A4 notepad and a thick black marker, Take the Risk if she has it, a phone case for the maximizer example
record.wear: A plain solid top that contrasts with the wall

ideas.script:
### Open

You literally want to do everything, so you end up doing nothing.

And this is a loop that you have to force yourself to break out of.

It has a name. It's called decision paralysis.

*[on screen: Decision paralysis]*

I'll show you the four questions I use when I'm stuck, which I read in a Ben Carson book when I was a teenager. And I'll tell you what I did when I wanted to learn how to ride a bike, because the usual me would have done it the wrong way.

### What decision paralysis is

Decision paralysis is when you have a decision to make, and you get so stuck thinking about it that you don't decide at all.

Some people also call it analysis paralysis.

For example, say you want to start a YouTube channel, and you also want to learn French, and you also want to get fit, and you also want to finally start building that side project.

So you open 10 tabs comparing different cameras for your YouTube channel.

And you watch three different videos on which language app is best for you to learn French.

And you check all the gym prices, because you want to get fit.

And at the end of the week, you haven't started any of those things that you said you want to start.

It's a loop. You want to do everything, you can't pick, so you do nothing.

*[draw the loop on the notepad while you say this and the next line; hold it up]*

Then you feel bad about doing nothing, and next week your list is even longer.

There's an old fable that I read. It's about a fox and a cat.

It's one of Aesop's fables, usually called The Fox and the Cat.

*[on screen: fox and cat]*

The fox brags that he has hundreds of ways to escape when the hunters' dogs come.

And the cat says that she only has one way to escape.

Then the dogs come, and the cat runs straight up a tree.

The fox, however, is still deciding which of his hundred ways to use, and obviously the dogs catch him.

It's very interesting, because the fox had the most options, but he was still the one who got caught.

So if you stay in that decision paralysis loop long enough, doing nothing will slowly become your habit.

And you might start to think that you're lazy, but it didn't start as laziness.

### Maximizers and satisficers

Some people get stuck on decisions more than others, and researchers have a name for these two sides.

Maximizers and satisficers. Try to check which one you are.

*[on screen: Maximizer / Satisficer]*

A satisficer looks until they find something good enough, and then they stop.

A maximizer wants the best possible option, so they keep looking.

So say you want to buy a phone case.

*[hold up a phone case]*

The satisficer wants a black phone case that fits, that is under 20 euros, and they buy the first one that ticks all of those boxes.

A maximizer, however, will read every single review and check different shops, and then eventually buy one.

And then they see a better one the next week, and then they feel bad about it.

If you're like me, you sometimes just want to do everything.

And wanting to do every single thing the best way is a lot of load to carry.

So I would be a maximizer about a few things that matter to me, but I'm learning to be a satisficer about the rest.

And in a bit I'll show you the four questions I use when I'm stuck like this.

### Why doing nothing feels safer

When you're stuck on a decision, doing nothing feels like a safe choice.

Say you start the business and it fails. That feels like your fault.

If you never start it, nothing happened, so it doesn't feel like anybody's fault.

And that safe feeling is part of what keeps the loop going.

### Is decision paralysis the same as decision fatigue?

Is decision paralysis the same as decision fatigue?

A lot of people blame decision paralysis on decision fatigue.

Decision fatigue is the idea that making a lot of decisions wears you out.

So let's just talk about it. Is it the same thing? Are they connected? Are you stuck because you've used up your decision energy?

I don't think they're the same thing.

Decision fatigue is about being tired after making a lot of decisions.

Decision paralysis is being stuck on a decision, so you don't make it at all.

But I do think they can be connected.

Say you've had a long day at work, and you've been making small decisions since morning.

Then at night, you sit down to decide if you should start learning French, and it feels a lot heavier than it should.

So being tired can make the loop worse.

But you can also wake up rested on a Saturday morning, with nothing else to decide, and still be stuck on that same decision.

So I wouldn't say you're stuck just because you've used up your decision energy for the day.

People argue a lot about how much decision fatigue really explains, so I wouldn't lean on it too much.

For me, it's usually that I want to do everything, and I can't pick.

Being tired doesn't help, though, so I try to make my big decisions when I'm rested.

### How to stop overthinking a decision: Ben Carson's four questions

Let's get to the practical part, how to stop overthinking a decision.

If you're stuck overthinking a decision, this is what I do to make the decision.

For me, I always try to get to the results, like how helpful that decision is.

Because when you slack on a decision, at least for me, I think it's usually because it sounds like a good idea, but you're not very convinced about how effective or productive it is.

And you could slack on a decision because of that, but you might not be able to tell yourself that.

So for me, I always do this four-question thing.

I read it in a Ben Carson book when I was a teenager.

The book is called Take the Risk, and he calls this a best/worst analysis.

*[book on camera or pasted cover + THINKER CARD: Ben Carson, Take the Risk, 2008]*

He says he would ask himself four questions.

*[draw the 2×2 grid as you say them; a PHRASE CARD for each]*

What is the best thing that can happen if I do this?

What is the worst thing that can happen if I do this?

What is the best thing that can happen if I don't do it?

What is the worst thing that can happen if I don't do it?

I think for me, it always forces me to face the enormity, the size or the impact, of that decision that I want to make.

Is it going to be so impactful? Is it going to be impactful in a positive way, or in a negative way? Or is it going to be just one of those things?

And when I do this, it always helps me cut down the options.

### How to break the loop and start

To break the loop of doing nothing, you have to start.

And these are three things I will do.

The first one is to pick one thing, and park the rest on the list.

*[on screen: First]*

A lot of people love to call themselves multipotentialites, right? And I do think of myself as one of those.

I have interests in a lot of things, and I think I do a lot of things well.

And I've also switched between a lot of things in my life.

And those switches were not me giving up on things. I don't think so.

I have different interests, and I think I flourish at different things.

But I would say, if you're stuck in this loop of decision paralysis, pick one single thing and park the rest for now.

If I want to start four new things this month, there's no amount of planning that will help me, because I wouldn't get anything done.

I'm already too busy for four new things.

So pick one, put the rest on the list, and look at it later.

The second thing is to find the smallest next action.

*[on screen: Second]*

I remember when I wanted to learn how to ride a bike.

I just wanted to do something physical and go out, and I'm like, yeah, what's the smallest thing I could do?

Well, I could try to buy a bike.

Or I could just borrow my neighbour's bike.

So find the smallest next action, right?

As David Allen puts it in his book Getting Things Done, the next action is the next physical, visible activity.

*[on screen: David Allen, Getting Things Done]*

For example, "learn French" is too big an action.

But "download an app to learn French and do lesson one", that seems like something you can do now.

And the third one is what actually got me on that bike.

*[only if true, see question 1]*

And also, if you want to really make it happen, attach it to a time and a place.

*[on screen: Third]*

Again, using my bike riding example, I told myself that week, I'm going to learn how to ride a bike this week.

Because I also do this terrible thing where, if I want to do something, the first thing I'm always thinking of is ways to spend money.

Like, the usual me would want to buy a bike first.

But yeah, I borrowed my neighbour's bike, and I just put it up on Facebook.

Like, "Hey guys, everybody here that I do not know, I need to learn to ride a bike, and I need to learn to ride this bike this week."

*[space for one line in your words on how it ended, see question 1.]*

So if you really want to make it happen, attach a time and a place to it.

It's called an implementation intention. "7pm on Tuesday, I will do lesson one."

So your decision paralysis loop will not break on its own.

You have to force it to break by doing one small thing.

What's one decision you've been stuck on for too long? Write it in the comments, and write the smallest next action next to it.

*[outro: record both, we use the one that fits]*

A: If what keeps you stuck is your phone, I made a whole video on why you can't stop scrolling. It's right here.

B: And if you've noticed you don't sit with questions anymore, watch my video on whether AI is making us less curious.

ideas.title: Is AI Making Us Less Curious? Googling vs Asking AI
ideas.format: Talking head in a calm new spot + black phrase cards (#29) + a thinker card for Loewenstein and a further-reading end card (#26) + one Pew receipt; serif captions on black boxes
ideas.length: 5-6 min (8-9 if she brings back one old segment)
ideas.hook: Everyone keeps asking if AI is making us dumber. The question I keep coming back to is whether it's making us less curious.

record.where: Not the desk: a sofa or armchair by the biggest window, light from the side, a bookshelf or a plain wall with one warm lamp behind
record.how: Sitting, centred, eye-level camera about 1.2-1.5 m away, 4K landscape head and chest with room on both sides for the 9:16 crop; calm, like explaining over tea; the first 30 s twice
record.props: Her phone (a real screen recording of asking Claude something), a notebook or sticky note, an old dictionary or library book if she has one
record.wear: A plain solid top, no small stripes or logos

ideas.script:
### Is AI making us less curious?

Everyone keeps asking if AI is making us dumber. The question I keep coming back to is whether it's making us less curious.

*[on screen: We need to bring back curiosity]*

We need to bring back curiosity.

We need to bring back the "I don't know" state of mind.

The "I don't know" state of mind is what fuels curiosity.

And that "I don't know" state of mind is disappearing.

And it has a lot to do with that feeling when someone is telling you gist, and then they stop and say, "I'll tell you later." I'll come back to that.

There was a time we didn't have this easy access to knowledge or information.

*[on screen: ChatGPT came out on 30 November 2022]*

Even as at four, five years ago, if you wanted to know something, you would have to search on Google, go through like different links, go through a few articles, a few posts, a few things about it, before you would come across it, like, oh yeah, yeah, it's this thing I'm looking for.

And before that, sometimes you'd have to go find a book about it, go to the library, or ask someone.

*[book on camera, 2 s]*

Sometimes you ask someone, they know a little bit, and then they point you to someone else, and then you talk to three people about it.

And you might get to know it at the end of all of that, or you might not get to know it.

But all of that is disappearing.

### Generative AI is filling the gap

And stay with me, because at the end I'll tell you what I actually think we've lost, and it's a small thing.

Generative AI is just completely filling that gap.

If I don't know something, and I become conscious of the fact that I don't know it, I can just open Claude and prompt Claude, and boom, almost immediately, I can just get to know it.

*[on screen: her phone, typing a real question into Claude]*

Obviously, it is a good thing, because it helps us access information faster.

But I also think that it, in turn, decreases the curious state of our mind.

It decreases curiosity because the "I don't know" state, that state where you don't know something, where you want to know something, you're trying to know something, is one of the states of mind that helps curiosity, that breeds curiosity.

And that state of mind is becoming more and more absent.

### What is curiosity?

*[on screen: Curiosity is the state of having an open question]*

Curiosity is the state of having an open question.

We are no longer having open questions.

Our questions are being consistently, immediately answered.

*[on screen: GEORGE LOEWENSTEIN on curiosity, "a form of cognitively induced deprivation that arises from the perception of a gap in knowledge or understanding." Psychological Bulletin, 1994]*

Curiosity, according to the words of the psychologist George Loewenstein, is a form of cognitively induced deprivation that arises from the perception of a gap in knowledge or understanding.

In plain words, you notice something that you don't know, and not knowing it feels like a little bit of hunger, and you want to fill it up.

It's like when someone is telling you gist, and then they stop and say, "I'll tell you later."

Now you cannot rest until they tell you.

Curiosity lives in the not knowing, in the half-knowing, in the semi-knowing.

You know enough to have a guess.

You know enough to know that you don't know, and now you're curious.

And that curiosity, that waiting, that open-endedness, it gets your brain ready in a way.

When our questions are answered in a second, it closes that gap too fast for us.

### Googling vs asking AI, and what we've lost

With Google, you can say that Googling was a form of getting an immediate answer.

But at least we had to click links and read different kind of stuff on different kind of sites.

But with generative AI, we don't even look at a list of links.

*[on screen: Pew Research, July 2025: a click on a result in 8 % of Google visits with an AI summary, 15 % without]*

We just get one answer that is already put together for us.

*[on screen: one answer, already put together]*

You can't even compare it to the Googling era, because then, when you search, you have to find the information and put it together for yourself.

The "I don't know" state.

I don't have a better word for it, but to call it an "I don't know" state of mind.

It used to last longer, in a way that it breeds curiosity well enough, but now it just lasts about as long as it takes to type a prompt.

And when I talk about this, it feels to me, even to me, if I wanna counter my own point, it feels to me like I'm romanticising ignorance, or not knowing something.

I think that access to information is really good.

In this age and time, AI is one of the best things that we have, and I'm grateful for it.

I don't want to go back to a time where I have a question and it just sits unanswered for months, or having to go into a library and search and search and search.

I don't want that either.

My point is the prolonged state of not knowing.

*[on screen: the prolonged state of not knowing]*

That is the thing that I feel like we have lost.

Not knowing something until I read like five articles that different people compile together, and I try to bring everything together, you know.

But that is no longer there.

What's a question you've been carrying around that you haven't looked up yet? Tell me in the comments.

*[outro: record both, we use the one that fits]*

A: If this made you think about how much of your attention goes to your phone, I made a whole video on why you can't stop scrolling. It's right here.

B: And if you're someone who wants to do everything and ends up doing nothing, I made a video on decision paralysis. Watch that one next.

ideas.script:
When your phone says "connected, no internet", it's telling you where the problem is.

*[on screen: a phone Wi-Fi screen with "Connected, no internet" under the network name (generic, not your real network)]*

Think of your home as a house. Wi-Fi is the hallway inside it. It connects your phone and your laptop to the router.

The router is the receptionist. It passes messages in and out for every device in the house.

The modem is the front gate, where the line from outside comes in. And your internet provider, the company you pay, owns the road from your gate to the rest of the internet.

*[on screen: flat diagram building up beside you: phone → hallway (Wi-Fi) → receptionist (router) → gate (modem) → road (your provider) → the internet. A MiFi drawn as router + modem in one small box.]*

So "connected, no internet" means your phone reached the receptionist. The problem is further out, at the gate, the line, or your provider.

If every device in the house has lost internet, restart the router and the modem. If it's only your phone, look at your phone.

And on hotel or school Wi-Fi, it often means you haven't signed in on their login page yet.
